entries.33ecaca044becbdee3b4411889b5b45f197da351: <div sID="gen31226" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="1Cor.11" sID="1Cor.11"/> <div eID="gen31226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31227" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31228" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle blames, and endeavours to rectify, some great indecencies and manifest disorders in the church of Corinth; as, I. The misconduct of their women (some of whom seem to have been inspired) in the public assembly, who laid by their veils, the common token of subjection to their husbands in that part of the world. This behaviour he reprehends, requires them to keep veiled, asserts the superiority of the husband, yet so as to remind the husband that both were made for mutual help and comfort, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1-Rom.11.16">ver. 1-16</reference>. II. He blames them for their discord and neglect and contempt of the poor, at the Lord's supper, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.17-Rom.11.22">ver. 17-22</reference>. III. To rectify these scandalous disorders, he sets before them the nature and intentions of this holy institution, directs them how they should attend on it, and warns them of the danger of a conduct to indecent as theirs, and of all unworthy receiving, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.23-Rom.11.34">ver. 23, to the end</reference>.
entries.f2202585460ead72590996aeaffa6ab5c8faa543: <div eID="gen31228" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31227" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Directions Concerning Attire; Female Subjection. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31229" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Be ye followers of me, even as I also <hi type="italic">am</hi> of Christ. <hi type="super">2</hi> Now I praise you, brethren, that ye remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances, as I delivered <hi type="italic">them</hi> to you. <hi type="super">3</hi> But I would have you know, that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man; and the head of Christ <hi type="italic">is</hi> God. <hi type="super">4</hi> Every man praying or prophesying, having <hi type="italic">his</hi> head covered, dishonoureth his head. <hi type="super">5</hi> But every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with <hi type="italic">her</hi> head uncovered dishonoureth her head: for that is even all one as if she were shaven. <hi type="super">6</hi> For if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn: but if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered. <hi type="super">7</hi> For a man indeed ought not to cover <hi type="italic">his</hi> head, forasmuch as he is the image and glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man. 8 For the man is not of the woman; but the woman of the man. 9 Neither was the man created for the woman; but the woman for the man. <hi type="super">10</hi> For this cause ought the woman to have power on <hi type="italic">her</hi> head because of the angels. <hi type="super">11</hi> Nevertheless neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord. <hi type="super">12</hi> For as the woman <hi type="italic">is</hi> of the man, even so <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man also by the woman; but all things of God. 13 Judge in yourselves: is it comely that a woman pray unto God uncovered? <hi type="super">14</hi> Doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him? <hi type="super">15</hi> But if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for <hi type="italic">her</hi> hair is given her for a covering. <hi type="super">16</hi> But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God. <div eID="gen31229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31230" type="x-p"/> Paul, having answered the cases put to him, proceeds in this chapter to the redress of grievances. The <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">first verse</reference> of the chapter is put, by those who divided the epistle into chapters, as a preface to the rest of the epistle, but seems to have been a more proper close to the last, in which he had enforced the cautions he had given against the abuse of liberty, by his own example: <hi type="italic">Be ye followers of me, as I also am of Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">v. 1</reference>), fitly closes his argument; and the way of speaking in the <reference osisRef="Rom.11.2">next verse</reference> looks like a transition to another. But, whether it more properly belong to this or the last chapter, it is plain from it that Paul not only preached such doctrine as they ought to believe, but led such a life as they ought to imitate. "Be ye followers of me," that is, "Be imitators of me; live as you see me live." Note, Ministers are likely to preach most to the purpose when they can press their hearers to follow their example. Yet would not Paul be followed blindly neither. He encourages neither implicit faith nor obedience. He would be followed himself no further than he followed Christ. Christ's pattern is a copy without a blot; so is no man's else. Note, We should follow no leader further than he follows Christ. Apostles should be left by us when they deviate from the example of their Master. He passes next to reprehend and reform an indecency among them, of which the women were more especially guilty, concerning which observe, <div eID="gen31230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31231" type="x-p"/> I. How he prefaces it. He begins with a commendation of what was praiseworthy in them (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">I praise you, that you remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances as I delivered them to you.</hi> Many of them, it is probable, did this in the strictest sense of the expression: and he takes occasion thence to address the body of the church under this good character; and the body might, in the main, have continued to observe the ordinances and institutions of Christ, though in some things they deviated from, and corrupted, them. Note, When we reprove what is amiss in any, it is very prudent and fit to commend what is good in them; it will show that the reproof is not from ill-will, and a humour of censuring and finding fault; and it will therefore procure the more regard to it. <div eID="gen31231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31232" type="x-p"/> II. How he lays the foundation for his reprehension by asserting the superiority of the man over the woman: <hi type="italic">I would have you know that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God.</hi> Christ, in his mediatorial character and glorified humanity, is at the head of mankind. He is not only first of the kind, but Lord and Sovereign. He has a name above every name: though in this high office and authority he has a superior, God being his head. And as God is the head of Christ, and Christ the head of the whole human kind, so the man is the head of the two sexes: not indeed with such dominion as Christ has over the kind or God has over the man Christ Jesus; but a superiority and headship he has, and the woman should be in subjection and not assume or usurp the man's place. This is the situation in which God has placed her; and for that reason she should have a mind suited to her rank, and not do any thing that looks like an affectation of changing places. Something like this the women of the church of Corinth seem to have been guilty of, who were under inspiration, and prayed and prophesied even in their assemblies, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">v. 5</reference>. It is indeed an apostolical canon, that the women <hi type="italic">should keep silence in the churches</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.34">ch. xiv. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.12">1 Tim. ii. 12</reference>), which some understand without limitation, as if a woman under inspiration also must keep silence, which seems very well to agree with the connection of the apostle's discourse, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.1-Rom.14.23">ch. xiv</reference>. Others with a limitation: though a woman might not from her own abilities pretend to teach, or so much as question and debate any thing in the church yet when under inspiration the case was altered, she had liberty to speak. Or, though she might not preach even by inspiration (because teaching is the business of a superior), yet she might pray or utter hymns by inspiration, even in the public assembly. She did not show any affectation of superiority over the man by such acts of public worship. It is plain the apostle does not in this place prohibit the thing, but reprehend the manner of doing it. And yet he might utterly disallow the thing and lay an unlimited restraint on the woman in another part of the epistle. These things are not contradictory. It is to his present purpose to reprehend the manner wherein the women prayed and prophesied in the church, without determining in this place whether they did well or ill in praying or prophesying. Note, The manner of doing a thing enters into the morality of it. We must not only be concerned to do good, but that the good we do be well done. <div eID="gen31232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31233" type="x-p"/> III. The thing he reprehends is the woman's praying or prophesying uncovered, or the man's doing either covered, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.4-Rom.11.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. To understand this, it must be observed that it was a signification either of shame or subjection for persons to be veiled, or covered, in the eastern countries, contrary to the custom of ours, where the being bare-headed betokens subjection, and being covered superiority and dominion. And this will help us the better to understand, <div eID="gen31233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31234" type="x-p"/> IV. The reasons on which he grounds his reprehension. 1. <hi type="italic">The man that prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonoureth his head,</hi> namely, Christ, the head of every man (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.3">v. 3</reference>), by appearing in a habit unsuitable to the rank in which God has placed him. Note, We should, even in our dress and habits, avoid every thing that may dishonour Christ. <hi type="italic">The woman,</hi> on the other hand, <hi type="italic">who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head,</hi> namely, the man, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.3">v. 3</reference>. She appears in the dress of her superior, and throws off the token of her subjection. She might, with equal decency, cut her hair short, or cut it close, which was the custom of the man in that age. This would be in a manner to declare that she was desirous of changing sexes, a manifest affectation of that superiority which God had conferred on the other sex. And this was probably the fault of these prophetesses in the church of Corinth. It was doing a thing which, in that age of the world, betokened superiority, and therefore a tacit claim of what did not belong to them but the other sex. Note, The sexes should not affect to change places. The order in which divine wisdom has placed persons and things is best and fittest: to endeavour to amend it is to destroy all order, and introduce confusion. The woman should keep to the rank God has chosen for her, and not dishonour her head; for this, in the result, is to dishonour God. If she was made out of the man, and for the man, and made to be the glory of the man, she should do nothing, especially in public, that looks like a wish of having this order inverted. 2. Another reason against this conduct is that <hi type="italic">the man is the image and glory of God,</hi> the representative of that glorious dominion and headship which God has over the world. It is the man who is set at the head of this lower creation, and therein he bears the resemblance of God. The woman, on the other hand, <hi type="italic">is the glory of the man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.7">v. 7</reference>): she is his representative. Not but she has dominion over the inferior creatures, as she is a partaker of human nature, and so far is God's representative too, but it is at second-hand. She is the image of God, inasmuch as she is the image of the man: <hi type="italic">For the man was not made out of the woman, but the woman out of the man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.8">v. 8</reference>. The man was first made, and made head of the creation here below, and therein the image of the divine dominion; and the woman was made out of the man, and shone with a reflection of his glory, being made superior to the other creatures here below, but in subjection to her husband, and deriving that honour from him out of whom she was made. 3. <hi type="italic">The woman was made for the man,</hi> to be his help-meet, <hi type="italic">and not the man for the woman.</hi> She was naturally, therefore, made subject to him, because made for him, for his use, and help, and comfort. And she who was intended to be always in subjection to the man should do nothing, in Christian assemblies, that looks like an affectation of equality. 4. <hi type="italic">She ought to have power on her head, because of the angels.</hi> Power, that is, a veil, the token, not of her having the power or superiority, but being under the power of her husband, subjected to him, and inferior to the other sex. Rebekah, when she met Isaac, and was delivering herself into his possession, put on her veil, in token of her subjection, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.65">Gen. xxiv. 65</reference>. Thus would the apostle have the women appear in Christian assemblies, even though they spoke there by inspiration, <hi type="italic">because of the angels,</hi> that is, say some, because of the evil angels. The woman <hi type="italic">was first in the transgression, being deceived by the devil</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.14">1 Tim. ii. 14</reference>), which increased her subjection to man, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Gen. iii. 16</reference>. Now, believe evil angels will be sure to mix in all Christian assemblies, therefore should women wear the token of their shamefacedness and subjection, which in that age and country, was a veil. Others say because of the good angels. Jews and Christians have had an opinion that these ministering spirits are many of them present in their assemblies. Their presence should restrain Christians from all indecencies in the worship of God. Note, We should learn from all to behave in the public assemblies of divine worship so as to express a reverence for God, and a content and satisfaction with that rank in which he has placed us. <div eID="gen31234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31235" type="x-p"/> V. He thinks fit to guard his argument with a caution lest the inference be carried too far (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.11-Rom.11.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Nevertheless, neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man in the Lord.</hi> They were made for one another. <hi type="italic">It is not good for him to be alone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.18">Gen. ii. 18</reference>), and therefore was a woman made, and made for the man; and the man was intended to be a comfort, and help, and defence, to the woman, though not so directly and immediately made for her. They were made to be a mutual comfort and blessing, not one a slave and the other a tyrant. <hi type="italic">Both were to be one flesh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.24">Gen. ii. 24</reference>), and this for the propagation of a race of mankind. They are reciprocal instruments of each other's production. As the woman was first formed out of the man, the man is ever since propagated by the woman (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.12">v. 12</reference>), all by the divine wisdom and power of the First Cause so ordaining it. The authority and subjection should be no greater than are suitable to two in such near relation and close union to each other. Note, As it is the will of God that the woman know her place, so it is his will also that the man abuse not his power. <div eID="gen31235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31236" type="x-p"/> VI. He enforces his argument from the natural covering provided for the woman (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.13-Rom.11.15">v. 13-15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Judge in yourselves</hi>—consult your own reason, hearken to what nature suggests—<hi type="italic">is it comely for a woman to pray to God uncovered?</hi> Should there not be a distinction kept up between the sexes in wearing their hair, since nature has made one? Is it not a distinction which nature has kept up among all civilized nations? The woman's hair is a natural covering; to wear it long is a glory to her; but for a man to have long hair, or cherish it, is a token of softness and effeminacy." Note, It should be our concern, especially in Christian and religious assemblies, to make no breach upon the rules of natural decency. <div eID="gen31236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31237" type="x-p"/> VII. He sums up all by referring those who were contentious to the usages and customs of the churches, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.16">v. 16</reference>. Custom is in a great measure the rule of decency. And the common practice of the churches is what he would have them govern themselves by. He does not silence the contentious by mere authority, but lets them know that they would appear to the world as very odd and singular in their humour if they would quarrel for a custom to which all the churches of Christ were at that time utter strangers, or against a custom in which they all concurred, and that upon the ground of natural decency. It was the common usage of the churches for women to appear in public assemblies, and join in public worship, veiled; and it was manifestly decent that they should do so. Those must be very contentious indeed who would quarrel with this, or lay it aside.
entries.d2f7c05fda32ad418216ffe12ef85ff86ff05def: <div eID="gen31237" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Profanation of the Lord's Supper. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31238" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Now in this that I declare <hi type="italic">unto you</hi> I praise <hi type="italic">you</hi> not, that ye come together not for the better, but for the worse. <hi type="super">18</hi> For first of all, when ye come together in the church, I hear that there be divisions among you; and I partly believe it. <hi type="super">19</hi> For there must be also heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you. <hi type="super">20</hi> When ye come together therefore into one place, <hi type="italic">this</hi> is not to eat the Lord's supper. <hi type="super">21</hi> For in eating every one taketh before <hi type="italic">other</hi> his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken. <hi type="super">22</hi> What? have ye not houses to eat and to drink in? or despise ye the church of God, and shame them that have not? What shall I say to you? shall I praise you in this? I praise <hi type="italic">you</hi> not. <div eID="gen31238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31239" type="x-p"/> In this passage the apostle sharply rebukes them for much greater disorders than the former, in their partaking of the Lord's supper, which was commonly done in the first ages, as the ancients tell us, with a love-feast annexed, which gave occasion to the scandalous disorders which the apostle here reprehends, concerning which observe, <div eID="gen31239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31240" type="x-p"/> I. The manner in which he introduces his charge: "<hi type="italic">Now in this that I declare to you I praise you not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">v. 17</reference>. I cannot commend, but must blame and condemn you." It is plain, from the beginning of the chapter, that he was willing and pleased to commend as far as he could. But such scandalous disorders, in so sacred an institution, as they were guilty of, called for a sharp reprehension. They quite turned the institution against itself. It was intended to make them better, to promote their spiritual interests; but it really made them worse. <hi type="italic">They came together, not for the better, but for the worse.</hi> Note, The ordinances of Christ, if they do not make us better, will be very apt to make us worse; if they do not do our souls good, they do us harm; if they do not melt and mend, they will harden. Corruptions will be confirmed in us, if the proper means do not work a cure of them. <div eID="gen31240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31241" type="x-p"/> II. He enters upon his charge against them in more particulars than one. 1. He tells them that, upon coming together, they fell into <hi type="italic">divisions, schisms</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">schismata.</hi></hi> Instead of concurring unanimously in celebrating the ordinance, they fell a quarrelling with one another. Note, There may be schism where there is no separation of communion. Persons may come together in the same church, and sit down at the same table of the Lord, and yet be schismatics. Uncharitableness, alienation of affection, especially if it grows up to discord, and feuds, and contentions, constitute schism. Christians may separate from each other's communion, and yet be uncharitable one towards another; they may continue in the same communion, and yet be uncharitable. This latter is schism, rather than the former. The apostle had heard a report of the Corinthians' divisions, and he tells them he had too much reason to believe it. For, adds he, there must be heresies also; not only quarrels, but factions, and perhaps such corrupt opinions as strike at the foundation of Christianity, and all sound religion. Note, No marvel there should be breaches of Christian love in the churches, when such offences will come as shall make shipwreck of faith and a good conscience. Such offences must come. Note that men are necessitated to be guilty of them; but the event is certain, and God permits them, that those who are approved (such honest hearts as will bear the trial) may be set to view, and appear faithful by their constant adherence to the truths and ways of God, notwithstanding the temptations of seducers. Note, The wisdom of God can make the wickedness and errors of others a foil to the piety and integrity of the saints. 2. He charges them not only with discord and division, but with scandalous disorder: <hi type="italic">For in eating every one taketh before the other his own supper; and one is hungry, and another is drunken,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.21">v. 21</reference>. Heathens used to drink plentifully at their feasts upon their sacrifices. Many of the wealthier Corinthians seem to have taken the same liberty at the Lord's table, or at least at their <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Agapai,</hi></hi> or <hi type="italic">love-feasts,</hi> that were annexed to the supper. They would not stay for one another; the rich despised the poor, and ate and drank up the provisions they themselves brought, before the poor were allowed to partake; and thus some wanted, while others had more than enough. This was profaning a sacred institution, and corrupting a divine ordinance, to the last degree. What was appointed to feed the soul was employed to feed their lusts and passions. What should have been a bond of mutual amity and affection was made an instrument of discord and disunion. The poor were deprived of the food prepared for them, and the rich turned a feast of charity into a debauch. This was scandalous irregularity. <div eID="gen31241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31242" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle lays the blame of this conduct closely on them, 1. By telling them that their conduct perfectly destroyed the purpose and use of such an institution: <hi type="italic">This is not to eat the Lord's supper,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.20">v. 20</reference>. It was coming to the Lord's table, and not coming. They might as well have staid away. Thus to eat the outward elements was not to eat Christ's body. Note, There is a careless and irregular eating of the Lord's supper which is as none at all; it will turn to no account, but to increase guilt. Such an eating was that of the Corinthians; their practices were a direct contradiction to the purposes of this sacred institution. 2. Their conduct carried in it a contempt of God's house, or of the church, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.22">v. 22</reference>. If they had a mind to feast, they might do it at home in their own houses; but to come to the Lord's table, and cabal and quarrel, and keep the poor from their share of the provision there made for them as well as rich, was such an abuse of the ordinance, and such a contempt of the poorer members of the church more especially, as merited a very sharp rebuke. Such a behaviour tended much to the shame and discouragement of the poor, whose souls were as dear to Christ, and cost him as much, as those of the rich. Note, Common meals may be managed after a common manner, but religious feasts should be attended religiously. Note, also, It is a heinous evil, and severely to be censured, for Christians to treat their fellow-christians with contempt and insolence, but especially at the Lord's table. This is doing what they can to pour contempt on divine ordinances. And we should look carefully to it that nothing in our behaviour at the Lord's table have the appearance of contemning so sacred an institution.
entries.d7af95cfeaf3ca69f03fb1e4b94b31de2c403595: <div eID="gen31242" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Design of the Lord's Supper. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31243" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the <hi type="italic">same</hi> night in which he was betrayed took bread: <hi type="super">24</hi> And when he had given thanks, he brake <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me. 25 After the same manner also <hi type="italic">he took</hi> the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink <hi type="italic">it,</hi> in remembrance of me. 26 For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do show the Lord's death till he come. <hi type="super">27</hi> Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink <hi type="italic">this</hi> cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. <hi type="super">28</hi> But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of <hi type="italic">that</hi> bread, and drink of <hi type="italic">that</hi> cup. <hi type="super">29</hi> For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body. <hi type="super">30</hi> For this cause many <hi type="italic">are</hi> weak and sickly among you, and many sleep. <hi type="super">31</hi> For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged. <hi type="super">32</hi> But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world. <hi type="super">33</hi> Wherefore, my brethren, when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another. <hi type="super">34</hi> And if any man hunger, let him eat at home; that ye come not together unto condemnation. And the rest will I set in order when I come. <div eID="gen31243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31244" type="x-p"/> To rectify these gross corruptions and irregularities, the apostle sets the sacred institution here to view. This should be the rule in the reformation of all abuses. <div eID="gen31244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31245" type="x-p"/> I. He tells us how he came by the knowledge of it. He was not among the apostles at the first institution; but <hi type="italic">he had received from the Lord what he delivered to them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.23">v. 23</reference>. He had the knowledge of this matter by revelation from Christ: and what he had received he communicated, without varying from the truth a tittle, without adding or diminishing. <div eID="gen31245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31246" type="x-p"/> II. He gives us a more particular account of the institution than we meet with elsewhere. We have here an account, <div eID="gen31246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31247" type="x-p"/> 1. Of the author—our Lord Jesus Christ. The king of the church only has power to institute sacraments. <div eID="gen31247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31248" type="x-p"/> 2. The time of the institution: <hi type="italic">It was the very night wherein he was betrayed;</hi> just as he was entering on his sufferings which are therein to be commemorated. <div eID="gen31248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31249" type="x-p"/> 3. The institution itself. Our Saviour took bread, and when he had given thanks, or <hi type="italic">blessed</hi> (as it is in <reference osisRef="Matt.26.26">Matt. xxvi. 26</reference>), <hi type="italic">he broke, and said, Take, eat; this is my body, broken for you; this do in remembrance of me. And in like manner he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the New Testament in my blood; this do, as oft as you drink it, in remembrance of me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.24-Rom.11.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen31249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31250" type="x-p"/> (1.) The materials of this sacrament; both, [1.] As to the visible signs; these are bread and the cup, the former of which is called bread many times over in this passage, even after what the papists call consecration. What is eaten is called bread, though it be at the same time said to be <hi type="italic">the body of the Lord,</hi> a plain argument that the apostle knew nothing of their monstrous and absurd doctrine of transubstantiation. The latter is as plainly a part of this institution as words can make it. St. Matthew tells us, our Lord bade them all drink of it (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.27">ch. xxvi. 27</reference>), as if he would, by this expression, lay in a caveat against the papists' depriving the laity of the cup. Bread and the cup are both made use of, because it is a holy feast. Nor is it here, or any where, made necessary, that any particular liquor should be in the cup. In one evangelist, indeed, it is plain that wine was the liquor used by our Saviour, though it was, perhaps, mingled with water, according to the Jewish custom; <hi type="italic">vide</hi> Lightfoot on <reference osisRef="Matt.26.27">Matt. xxvi</reference>. But this by no means renders it unlawful to have a sacrament where persons cannot come at wine. In every place of scripture in which we have an account of this part of the institution it is always expressed by a figure. The cup is put for what was in it, without once specifying what the liquor was, in the words of the institution. [2.] The things signified by these outward signs; they are Christ's body and blood, his body broken, his blood shed, together with all the benefits which flow from his death and sacrifice: <hi type="italic">it is the New Testament in his blood.</hi> His blood is the seal and sanction of all the privileges of the new covenant; and worthy receivers take it as such, at this holy ordinance. They have the New Testament, and their own title to all the blessings of the new covenant, confirmed to them by his blood. <div eID="gen31250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31251" type="x-p"/> (2.) We have here the sacramental actions, the manner in which the materials of the sacrament are to be used. [1.] Our Saviour's actions, which are taking the bread and cup, giving thanks, breaking the bread, and giving about both the one and the other. [2.] The actions of the communicants, which were to take the bread and eat, to take the cup and drink, and both in remembrance of Christ. But the external acts are not the whole nor the principal part of what is to be done at this holy ordinance; each of them has a significancy. Our Saviour, having undertaken to make an offering of himself to God, and procure, by his death, the remission of sins, with all other gospel benefits, for true believers, did, at the institution, deliver his body and blood, with all the benefits procured by his death, to his disciples, and continues to do the same every time the ordinance is administered to the true believers. This is here exhibited, or set forth, as the food of souls. And as food, though ever so wholesome or rich, will yield no nourishment without being eaten, here the communicants are to take and eat, or to receive Christ and feed upon him, his grace and benefits, and by faith convert them into nourishment to their souls. They are to take him as their Lord and life, yield themselves up to him, and live upon him. <hi type="italic">He is our life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.4">Col. iii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen31251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31252" type="x-p"/> (3.) We have here an account of the ends of this institution. [1.] It was appointed to be done <hi type="italic">in remembrance of Christ,</hi> to keep fresh in our minds an ancient favour, his dying for us, as well as to remember an absent friend, even Christ interceding for us, in virtue of his death, at God's right hand. The best of friends, and the greatest acts of kindness, are here to be remembered, with the exercise of suitable affections and graces. The motto on this ordinance, and the very meaning of it, is, <hi type="italic">When this you see, remember me.</hi> [2.] It was <hi type="italic">to show forth Christ's death,</hi> to declare and publish it. It is not barely in remembrance of Christ, of what he has done and suffered, that this ordinance was instituted; but to commemorate, to celebrate, his glorious condescension and grace in our redemption. We declare his death to be our life, the spring of all our comforts and hopes. And we glory in such a declaration; we show forth his death, and spread it before God, as our accepted sacrifice and ransom. We set it in view of our own faith, for our own comfort and quickening; and we own before the world, by this very service, that we are the disciples of Christ, who trust in him alone for salvation and acceptance with God. <div eID="gen31252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31253" type="x-p"/> (4.) It is moreover hinted here, concerning this ordinance, [1.] That it should be frequent: <hi type="italic">As often as you eat this bread,</hi> &c. Our bodily meals return often; we cannot maintain life and health without this. And it is fit that this spiritual diet should be taken often tool The ancient churches celebrated this ordinance every Lord's day, if not every day when they assembled for worship. [2.] That it must be perpetual. It is to be celebrated <hi type="italic">till the Lord shall come;</hi> till he shall come the second time, without sin, for the salvation of those that believe, and to judge the world. This is our warrant for keeping this feast. It was our Lord's will that we should thus celebrate the memorials of his death and passion, till he come in his own glory, and the Father's glory, with his holy angels, and put an end to the present state of things, and his own mediatorial administration, by passing the final sentence. Note, The Lord's supper is not a temporary, but a standing and perpetual ordinance. <div eID="gen31253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31254" type="x-p"/> III. He lays before the Corinthians the danger of receiving unworthily, of prostituting this institution as they did, and using it to the purposes of feasting and faction, with intentions opposite to its design, or a temper of mind altogether unsuitable to it; or keeping up the covenant with sin and death, while they are there professedly renewing and confirming their covenant with God. 1. It is great guilt which such contract. They shall <hi type="italic">be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.27">v. 27</reference>), of violating this sacred institution, of despising his body and blood. They act as if they <hi type="italic">counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith they are sanctified, an unholy thing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.29">Heb. x. 29</reference>. They profane the institution, and in a manner crucify their Saviour over again. Instead of being cleansed by his blood, they are guilty of his blood. 2. It is a great hazard which they run: <hi type="italic">They eat and drink judgment to themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.29">v. 29</reference>. They provoke God, and are likely to bring down punishment on themselves. No doubt but they incur great guilt, and so render themselves liable to damnation, to spiritual judgments and eternal misery. Every sin is in its own nature damning; and therefore surely so heinous a sin as profaning such a holy ordinance is so. And it is profaned in the grossest sense by such irreverence and rudeness as the Corinthians were guilty of. But fearful believers should not be discouraged from attending at this holy ordinance by the sound of these words, as if they bound upon themselves the sentence of damnation by coming to the table of the Lord unprepared. Thus sin, as well as all others, leaves room for forgiveness upon repentance; and the Holy Spirit never indited this passage of scripture to deter serious Christians from their duty, though the devil has often made this advantage of it, and robbed good Christians of their choicest comforts. The Corinthians came to the Lord's table as to a common feast, <hi type="italic">not discerning the Lord's body</hi>—not making a difference or distinction between that and common food, but setting both on a level: nay, they used much more indecency at this sacred feast than they would have done at a civil one. This was very sinful in them, and very displeasing to God, and brought down his judgments on them: <hi type="italic">For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep.</hi> Some were punished with sickness, and some with death. Note, A careless and irreverent receiving of the Lord's supper may bring temporal punishments. Yet the connection seems to imply that even those who were thus punished were in a state of favour with God, at least many of them: <hi type="italic">They were chastened of the Lord, that they should not be condemned with the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.32">v. 32</reference>. Now divine chastening is a sign of divine love: <hi type="italic">Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.6">Heb. xii. 6</reference>), especially with so merciful a purpose, to prevent their final condemnation. In the midst of judgment, God remembers mercy: he frequently punishes those whom he tenderly loves. It is kindness to use the rod to prevent the child's ruin. He will visit such iniquity as this under consideration with stripes, and yet make those stripes the evidence of his lovingkindness. Those were in the favour of God who yet so highly offended him in this instance, and brought down judgments on themselves; at least many of them were; for they were punished by him out of fatherly good-will, punished now that they might not perish for ever. Note, It is better to bear trouble in this world than to be miserable to eternity. And God punishes his people now, to prevent their eternal woe. <div eID="gen31254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31255" type="x-p"/> IV. He points out the duty of those who would come to the Lord's table. 1. In general: <hi type="italic">Let a man examine himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">v. 28</reference>), try and approve himself. Let him consider the sacred intention of this holy ordinance, its nature, and use, and compare his own views in attending on it and his disposition of mind for it; and, when he has approved himself to his own conscience in the sight of God, then let him attend. Such self-examination is necessary to a right attendance at this holy ordinance. Note, Those who, through weakness of understanding, cannot try themselves, are by no means fit to eat of this bread and drink of this cup; nor those who, upon a fair trial, have just ground to charge themselves with impenitency, unbelief, and alienation from the life of God. Those should have the wedding-garment on who would be welcome at this marriage-feast—grace in habit, and grace in exercise. 2. The duty of those who were yet unpunished for their profanation of this ordinance: <hi type="italic">If we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.31">v. 31</reference>. If we would thoroughly search and explore ourselves, and condemn and correct what we find amiss, we should prevent divine judgments. Note, To be exact and severe on ourselves and our own conduct is the most proper way in the world not to fall under the just severity of our heavenly Father. We must not judge others, lest we be judged (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.1">Matt. vii. 1</reference>); but we must judge ourselves, to prevent our being judged and condemned by God. We may be critical as to ourselves, but should be very candid in judging others. <div eID="gen31255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31256" type="x-p"/> V. He closes all with a caution against the irregularities of which they were guilty (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.33-Rom.11.34">v. 33, 34</reference>), charging them to avoid all indecency at the Lord's table. They were to eat for hunger and pleasure only at home, and not to change the holy supper to a common feast; and much less eat up the provisions before those who could bring none did partake of them, lest they should come together for condemnation. Note, Our holy duties, through our own abuse, may prove matter of condemnation. Christians may keep Sabbaths, hear sermons, attend at sacraments, and only aggravate guilt, and bring on a heavier doom. A sad but serious truth! O! let all look to it that they do not come together at any time to God's worship, and all the while provoke him, and bring down vengeance on themselves. Holy things are to be used in a holy manner, or else they are profaned. What else was amiss in this matter, he tells them, he would rectify when he came to them.  <chapter eID="1Cor.11"/> <div eID="gen31256" type="x-p"/>

entries.9fa277f096420f6d6cc381b176ce87ae8dfcc303: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16972"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <div sID="gen33542" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.1-1Cor.11.34">1Co 11:1-34</reference>. Censure on Disorders in Their Assemblies: Their Women Not Being Veiled, and Abuses at the Love-Feasts.<div eID="gen33542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16972"/>1. Rather belonging to the end of the tenth chapter, than to this chapter.<div eID="gen33543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">followers--</hi>Greek, "imitators."<div eID="gen33544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Christ--</hi>who did not please Himself (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.3">Ro 15:3</reference>); but gave Himself, at the cost of laying aside His divine glory, and dying as man, for us (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.2">Ep 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.4">Php 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>). We are to follow Christ first, and earthly teachers only so far as they follow Christ. <div eID="gen33545" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4a1f093937dcb51a301fe35502075cca9067349: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16973"/><div sID="gen33546" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16973"/>2. Here the chapter ought to begin.<div eID="gen33546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye remember me in all things--</hi>in your general practice, though in the particular instances which follow ye fail.<div eID="gen33547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ordinances--</hi>Greek, "traditions," that is, apostolic directions given by word of mouth or in writing (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">1Co 11:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.3">15:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.15">2Th 2:15</reference>). The reference here is mainly to ceremonies: for in <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">1Co 11:23</reference>, as to the Lord's Supper, which is not a mere ceremony, he says, not merely, "I delivered unto you," but also, "I received of the Lord"; here he says only, "I delivered to you." Romanists argue hence for oral traditions. But the difficulty is to know what is a genuine apostolic tradition intended for all ages. Any that can be proved to be such ought to be observed; any that cannot, ought to be rejected (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.18">Re 22:18</reference>). Those preserved in the written word alone can be proved to be such. <div eID="gen33548" type="x-p"/>
entries.59d81d2e226f780583189f10f19339cb55a114ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16974"/><div sID="gen33549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16974"/>3. The Corinthian women, on the ground of the abolition of distinction of sexes in Christ, claimed equality with the male sex, and, overstepping the bounds of propriety, came forward to pray and prophesy without the customary head-covering of females. The Gospel, doubtless, did raise women from the degradation in which they had been sunk, especially in the East. Yet, while on a level with males as to the offer of, and standing in grace (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Ga 3:28</reference>), their subjection in point of order, modesty, and seemliness, is to be maintained. Paul reproves here their unseemliness as to dress: in <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Co 14:34</reference>, as to the retiring modesty in public which becomes them. He grounds his reproof here on the subjection of woman to man in the order of creation.<div eID="gen33549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the head--</hi>an appropriate expression, when he is about to treat of woman's appropriate headdress in public.<div eID="gen33550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33551" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of every man ... Christ--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.5.23">Ep 5:23</reference>).<div eID="gen33551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of ... woman ... man--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.8">1Co 11:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Ge 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.1">1Pe 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.6">5, 6</reference>).<div eID="gen33552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">head of Christ is God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.23">1Co 3:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.27">15:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.3.22">Lu 3:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.38">38</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.28">Joh 14:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.17">20:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.9">Ep 3:9</reference>). "Jesus, therefore, must be of the same essence as God: for, since the man is the head of the woman, and since the head is of the same essence as the body, and God is the head of the Son, it follows the Son is of the same essence as the Father" [Chrysostom]. "The woman is of the essence of the man, and not made by the man; so, too, the Son is not made by the Father, but of the essence of the Father" [Theodoret, t. 3, p. 171]. <div eID="gen33553" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a2b44b905c008d069efe04b83ebe51c57d6b67b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16975"/><div sID="gen33554" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16975"/><hi type="bold">4. praying--</hi>in public (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.17">1Co 11:17</reference>).<div eID="gen33554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33555" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prophesying--</hi>preaching in the Spirit (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.10">1Co 12:10</reference>).<div eID="gen33555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having--</hi>that is, if he were to have: a supposed case to illustrate the impropriety in the woman's case. It was the Greek custom (and so that at Corinth) for men in worship to be uncovered; whereas the Jews wore the Talith, or veil, to show reverence before God, and their unworthiness to look on Him (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.2">Is 6:2</reference>); however, Maimonides [Mishna] excepts cases where (as in Greece) the custom of the place was different.<div eID="gen33556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dishonoureth his head--</hi>not as Alford, "Christ" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.3">1Co 11:3</reference>); but literally, as "his head" is used in the beginning of the verse. He dishonoreth his head (the principal part of the body) by wearing a covering or veil, which is a mark of subjection, and which makes him look downwards instead of upwards to his Spiritual Head, Christ, to whom alone he owes subjection. Why, then, ought not man to wear the covering in token of his subjection to Christ, as the woman wears it in token of her subjection to man? "Because Christ is not seen: the man is seen; so the covering of him who is under Christ is not seen; of her who is under the man, is seen" [Bengel]. (Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.7">1Co 11:7</reference>). <div eID="gen33557" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d43d385c1d537a2a25d639246349326a0bbfa74: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16976"/><div sID="gen33558" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16976"/><hi type="bold">5. woman ... prayeth ... prophesieth--</hi>This instance of women speaking in public worship is an extraordinary case, and justified only by the miraculous gifts which such women possessed as their credentials; for instance, Anna the prophetess and Priscilla (so <reference osisRef="Acts.2.18">Ac 2:18</reference>). The ordinary rule to them is: silence in public (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Co 14:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.35">35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>). Mental receptivity and activity in family life are recognized in Christianity, as most accordant with the destiny of woman. This passage does not necessarily sanction women speaking in public, even though possessing miraculous gifts; but simply records what took place at Corinth, without expressing an opinion on it, reserving the censure of it till <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Co 14:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.35">35</reference>. Even those women endowed with prophecy were designed to exercise their gift, rather in other times and places, than the public congregation.<div eID="gen33558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33559" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dishonoureth ... head--</hi>in that she acts against the divine ordinance and the modest propriety that becomes her: in putting away the veil, she puts away the badge of her subjection to man, which is her true "honor"; for through him it connects her with Christ, the head of the man. Moreover, as the head-covering was the emblem of maiden modesty before man (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.65">Ge 24:65</reference>), and conjugal chastity (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.16">Ge 20:16</reference>); so, to uncover the head indicated withdrawal from the power of the husband, whence a suspected wife had her head uncovered by the priest (<reference osisRef="Num.5.18">Nu 5:18</reference>). Alford takes "her head" to be man, her symbolical, not her literal head; but as it is literal in the former clause, it must be so in the latter one.<div eID="gen33559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all one as if ... shaven--</hi>As woman's hair is given her by nature, as her covering (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.15">1Co 11:15</reference>), to cut it off like a man, all admit, would be indecorous: therefore, to put away the head-covering, too, like a man, would be similarly indecorous. It is natural to her to have long hair for her covering: she ought, therefore, to add the other (the wearing of a head-covering) to show that she does of her own will that which nature itself teaches she ought to do, in token of her subjection to man. <div eID="gen33560" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d660b6ca46fb2233349b00bcc566559bdef85ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16977"/><div sID="gen33561" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16977"/>6. A woman would not like to be "shorn" or (what is worse) "shaven"; but if she chooses to be uncovered (unveiled) in front, let her be so also behind, that is, "shorn."<div eID="gen33561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33562" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a shame--</hi>an unbecoming thing (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.13-1Cor.11.15">1Co 11:13-15</reference>). Thus the shaving of nuns is "a shame." <div eID="gen33562" type="x-p"/>
entries.9bcf036d6498af5b4f2e10ad419a9b77177191e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16978"/><div sID="gen33563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16978"/>7-9. Argument, also, from man's more immediate relation to God, and the woman's to man.<div eID="gen33563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he is ... image ... glory of God--</hi>being created in God's "image," first and directly: the woman, subsequently, and indirectly, through the mediation of man. Man is the representative of God's "glory" this ideal of man being realized most fully in the Son of man (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.4">Psa 8:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.23">2Co 8:23</reference>). Man is declared in Scripture to be both the "image," and in the "likeness," of God (compare <reference osisRef="Jas.3.9">Jas 3:9</reference>). But "image" alone is applied to the Son of God (<reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">He 1:3</reference>). "Express image," Greek, "the impress." The Divine Son is not merely "like" God, He is God of God, "being of one substance (essence) with the Father." [Nicene Creed].<div eID="gen33564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33565" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">woman ... glory of ... man--</hi>He does not say, also, "the image of the man." For the sexes differ: moreover, the woman is created in the image of God, as well as the man (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.26">Ge 1:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">27</reference>). But as the moon in relation to the sun (<reference osisRef="Gen.37.9">Ge 37:9</reference>), so woman shines not so much with light direct from God, as with light derived from man, that is, in her order in creation; not that she does not in grace come individually into direct communion with God; but even here much of her knowledge is mediately given her through man, on whom she is naturally dependent. <div eID="gen33565" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d555526881b509bce67174380c5e23dea07c447: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16981"/><div sID="gen33568" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16981"/><hi type="bold">10. power on her head--</hi>the kerchief: French couvre chef, head-covering, the emblem of "power on her head"; the sign of her being under man's power, and exercising delegated authority under him. Paul had before his mind the root-connection between the Hebrew terms for "veil" (radid), and "subjection" (radad).<div eID="gen33568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33569" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of the angels--</hi>who are present at our Christian assemblies (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.138.1">Psa 138:1</reference>, "gods," that is, angels), and delight in the orderly subordination of the several ranks of God's worshippers in their respective places, the outward demeanor and dress of the latter being indicative of that inward humility which angels know to be most pleasing to their common Lord (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1Co 4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Ep 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.6">Ec 5:6</reference>). Hammond quotes Chrysostom, "Thou standest with angels; thou singest with them; thou hymnest with them; and yet dost thou stand laughing?" Bengel explains, "As the angels are in relation to God, so the woman is in relation to man. God's face is uncovered; angels in His presence are veiled (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.2">Is 6:2</reference>). Man's face is uncovered; woman in His presence is to be veiled. For her not to be so, would, by its indecorousness, offend the angels (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.10">Mt 18:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.31">31</reference>). She, by her weakness, especially needs their ministry; she ought, therefore, to be the more careful not to offend them." <div eID="gen33569" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb997dd1428fda639d98905a96b353497c90bff2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16982"/><div sID="gen33570" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16982"/>11. Yet neither sex is insulated and independent of the other in the Christian life [Alford]. The one needs the other in the sexual relation; and in respect to Christ ("in the Lord"), the man and the woman together (for neither can be dispensed with) realize the ideal of redeemed humanity represented by the bride, the Church. <div eID="gen33570" type="x-p"/>
entries.c35b09aab1ab111cbb7aa599d7de70a987da8f84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16983"/><div sID="gen33571" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16983"/>12. As the woman was formed out of (from) the man, even so is man born by means of woman; but all things (including both man and woman) are from God as their source (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.36">Ro 11:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18">2Co 5:18</reference>). They depend mutually each on the other, and both on him. <div eID="gen33571" type="x-p"/>
entries.72f51c8a0d51a30cc6b8ed874a39831aefe9fcf3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16984"/><div sID="gen33572" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16984"/>13. Appeal to their own sense of decorum.<div eID="gen33572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33573" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a woman ... unto God--</hi>By rejecting the emblem of subjection (the head-covering), she passes at one leap in praying publicly beyond both the man and angels [Bengel]. <div eID="gen33573" type="x-p"/>
entries.b93bafc7ed507331ae926d3a1256bd4a239966bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16985"/><div sID="gen33574" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16985"/>14. The fact that nature has provided woman, and not man, with long hair, proves that man was designed to be uncovered, and woman covered. The Nazarite, however, wore long hair lawfully, as being part of a vow sanctioned by God (<reference osisRef="Num.6.5">Nu 6:5</reference>). Compare as to Absalom, <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.26">2Sa 14:26</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Acts.18.18">Ac 18:18</reference>. <div eID="gen33574" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d933d2823914c8990db1cdb2bb2713cef5a9a02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16986"/><div sID="gen33575" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16986"/><hi type="bold">15. her hair ... for a covering--</hi>Not that she does not need additional covering. Nay, her long hair shows she ought to cover her head as much as possible. The will ought to accord with nature [Bengel]. <div eID="gen33575" type="x-p"/>
entries.9782c4e42f4defd30bfc1c3ddd46a320f085a012: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16987"/><div sID="gen33576" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16987"/>16. A summary close to the argument by appeal to the universal custom of the churches.<div eID="gen33576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if any ... seem--</hi>The Greek also means "thinks" (fit) (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.3.9">Mt 3:9</reference>). If any man chooses (still after all my arguments) to be contentious. If any be contentious and thinks himself right in being so. A reproof of the Corinthians' self-sufficiency and disputatiousness (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">1Co 1:20</reference>).<div eID="gen33577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we--</hi>apostles: or we of the Jewish nation, from whom ye have received the Gospel, and whose usages in all that is good ye ought to follow: <hi type="bold">Jewish women veiled themselves when in public, according to Tertullian [Estius]. The former explanation is best, as the Jews are not referred to in the context: but he often refers to himself and his fellow apostles, by the expression, "we--</hi>us" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1Co 4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen33578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33579" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no such custom--</hi>as that of women praying uncovered. Not as Chrysostom, "that of being contentious." The Greek term implies a usage, rather than a mental habit (<reference osisRef="John.18.39">Joh 18:39</reference>). The usage of true "churches (plural: not, as Rome uses it, 'the Church,' as an abstract entity; but 'the churches,' as a number of independent witnesses) of God" (the churches which God Himself recognizes), is a valid argument in the case of external rites, especially, negatively, for example, Such rites were not received among them, therefore, ought not to be admitted among us: but in questions of doctrine, or the essentials of worship, the argument is not valid [Sclater] (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.17">1Co 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.33">14:33</reference>).<div eID="gen33579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither--</hi>nor yet. Catholic usage is not an infallible test of truth, but a general test of decency. <div eID="gen33580" type="x-p"/>
entries.f73f8513316178eaadbecd6cdbc8bea69e81f288: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16988"/><div sID="gen33581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16988"/><hi type="bold">17. in this--</hi>which follows.<div eID="gen33581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I declare--</hi>rather, "I enjoin"; as the Greek is always so used. The oldest manuscripts read literally "This I enjoin (you) not praising (you)."<div eID="gen33582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33583" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that--</hi>inasmuch as; in that you, &c. Here he qualifies his praise (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.2">1Co 11:2</reference>). "I said that I praised you for keeping the ordinances delivered to you; but I must now give injunction in the name of the Lord, on a matter in which I praise you not; namely, as to the Lord's Supper (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">1Co 11:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.37">1Co 14:37</reference>).<div eID="gen33583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33584" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not for the better--</hi>not so as to progress to what is better.<div eID="gen33584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the worse--</hi>so as to retrograde to what is worse. The result of such "coming together" must be "condemnation" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.34">1Co 11:34</reference>). <div eID="gen33585" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3a30c3c2a74e58af9056053c6e9c71bae9245f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16989"/><div sID="gen33586" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16989"/><hi type="bold">18. first of all--</hi>In the first place. The "divisions" (Greek, "schisms") meant, are not merely those of opinion (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">1Co 1:10</reference>), but in outward acts at the love-feasts (Agapæ), (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.21">1Co 11:21</reference>). He does not follow up the expression, "in the first place," by "in the second place." But though not expressed, a second abuse was in his mind when he said, "In the first place," namely, THE ABUSE OF SPIRITUAL GIFTS, which also created disorder in their assemblies [Alford], (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.1">1Co 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.23">14:23</reference>, 26, 33, 40).<div eID="gen33586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33587" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the church--</hi>not the place of worship; for Isidore of Pelusium denies that there were such places specially set apart for worship in the apostles' times [Epistle, 246.2]. But, "in the assembly" or "congregation"; in convocation for worship, where especially love, order, and harmony should prevail. The very ordinance instituted for uniting together believers in one body, was made an occasion of "divisions" (schisms).<div eID="gen33587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33588" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">partly--</hi>He hereby excepts the innocent. "I am unwilling to believe all I hear, but some I cannot help believing" [Alford]: while my love is unaffected by it [Bengel]. <div eID="gen33588" type="x-p"/>
entries.dda6f5538f7af36404b5c9d1907bb7eefdb4b7ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16990"/><div sID="gen33589" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16990"/><hi type="bold">19. heresies--</hi>Not merely "schisms" or "divisions" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.18">1Co 11:18</reference>), which are "recent dissensions of the congregation through differences of opinion" [Augustine, Con. Crescon. Don. 2.7, quoted by Trench, Greek Synonyms of the New Testament], but also "heresies," that is, "schisms which have now become inveterate"; "Sects" [Campbell, vol. 2, pp. 126, 127]: so <reference osisRef="Acts.5.17">Ac 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.5">15:5</reference> translate the same Greek. At present there were dissensions at the love-feasts; but Paul, remembering Jesus' words (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.7">Mt 18:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.10">24:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.17.1">Lu 17:1</reference>) foresees "there must be (come) also" matured separations, and established parties in secession, as separatists. The "must be" arises from sin in professors necessarily bearing its natural fruits: these are overruled by God to the probation of character of both the godly and the ungodly, and to the discipline of the former for glory. "Heresies" had not yet its technical sense ecclesiastically, referring to doctrinal errors: it means confirmed schisms. St. Augustine's rule is a golden rule as regards questions of heresy and catholicity: "In doubtful questions, liberty; in essentials, unity; in all things, charity."<div eID="gen33589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that ... approved may be made manifest--</hi>through the disapproved (reprobates) becoming manifested (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.35">Lu 2:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.19">1Jo 2:19</reference>). <div eID="gen33590" type="x-p"/>
entries.190e6f06555ab3ec27cd1cedf22373e26012c514: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16991"/><div sID="gen33591" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16991"/><hi type="bold">20. When ... therefore--</hi>Resuming the thread of discourse from <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.18">1Co 11:18</reference>.<div eID="gen33591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33592" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this is not to--</hi>rather, "there is no such thing as eating the Lord's Supper"; it is not possible where each is greedily intent only on devouring "HIS OWN supper," and some are excluded altogether, not having been waited for (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.33">1Co 11:33</reference>), where some are "drunken," while others are "hungry" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.21">1Co 11:21</reference>). The love-feast usually preceded the Lord's Supper (as eating the Passover came before the Lord's Supper at the first institution of the latter). It was a club-feast, where each brought his portion, and the rich, extra portions for the poor; from it the bread and wine were taken for the Eucharist; and it was at it that the excesses took place, which made a true celebration of the Lord's Supper during or after it, with true discernment of its solemnity, out of the question. <div eID="gen33592" type="x-p"/>
entries.21dc507e3375c9f23082cdcd1947c2d51e3b6c55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16992"/><div sID="gen33593" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16992"/><hi type="bold">21. one taketh before other--</hi>the rich "before" the poor, who had no supper of their own. Instead of "tarrying for one another" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.33">1Co 11:33</reference>); hence the precept (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.21">1Co 12:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.25">25</reference>).<div eID="gen33593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33594" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his own supper--</hi>"His own" belly is his God (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>); "the Lord's Supper," the spiritual feast, never enters his thoughts.<div eID="gen33594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33595" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drunken--</hi>The one has more than is good for him, the other less [Bengel]. <div eID="gen33595" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac6721154f5740d4a0308bd033c12cf3c5774a31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16993"/><div sID="gen33596" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16993"/><hi type="bold">22. What!--</hi>Greek, "For."<div eID="gen33596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33597" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">houses--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.34">1Co 11:34</reference>)--"at home." That is the place to satiate the appetite, not the assembly of the brethren [Alford].<div eID="gen33597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">despise ye the church of God--</hi>the congregation mostly composed of the poor, whom "God hath chosen," however ye show contempt for them (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.5">Jas 2:5</reference>); compare "of God" here, marking the true honor of the Church.<div eID="gen33598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shame them that have not--</hi>namely, houses to eat and drink in, and who, therefore, ought to have received their portion at the love-feasts from their wealthier brethren.<div eID="gen33599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33600" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I praise you not--</hi>resuming the words (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.17">1Co 11:17</reference>). <div eID="gen33600" type="x-p"/>
entries.56349aef032561433a70015bed52c2b334ef1969: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16994"/><div sID="gen33601" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16994"/>23. His object is to show the unworthiness of such conduct from the dignity of the holy supper.<div eID="gen33601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33602" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I--</hi>Emphatic in the Greek. It is not my own invention, but the Lord's institution.<div eID="gen33602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33603" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">received of the Lord--</hi>by immediate revelation (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.12">Ga 1:12</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.22.17">Ac 22:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.22.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1-2Cor.12.4">2Co 12:1-4</reference>). The renewal of the institution of the Lord's Supper by special revelation to Paul enhances its solemnity. The similarity between Luke's and Paul's account of the institution, favors the supposition that the former drew his information from the apostle, whose companion in travel he was. Thus, the undesigned coincidence is a proof of genuineness.<div eID="gen33603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">night--</hi>the time fixed for the Passover (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.6">Ex 12:6</reference>): though the time for the Lord's Supper is not fixed.<div eID="gen33604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">betrayed--</hi>With the traitor at the table, and death present before His eyes, He left this ordinance as His last gift to us, to commemorate His death. Though about to receive such an injury from man, He gave this pledge of His amazing love to man. <div eID="gen33605" type="x-p"/>
entries.93526fc336203ccf8d03fc21d6160284c33f98cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16995"/><div sID="gen33606" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16995"/><hi type="bold">24. brake--</hi>The breaking of the bread involves its distribution and reproves the Corinthian mode at the love-feast, of "every one taking before other his own supper."<div eID="gen33606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33607" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my body ... broken for you--</hi>"given" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.19">Lu 22:19</reference>) for you (Greek, "in your behalf"), and "broken," so as to be distributed among you. The oldest manuscripts omit "broken," leaving it to be supplied from "brake." The two old versions, Memphitic and Thebaic, read from Luke, "given." The literal "body" could not have been meant; for Christ was still sensibly present among His disciples when He said, "This is My body." They could only have understood Him symbolically and analogically: As this bread is to your bodily health, so My body is to the spiritual health of the believing communicant. The words, "Take, eat," are not in the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen33607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in remembrance of me--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.25">1Co 11:25</reference>). <div eID="gen33608" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ec7d2097394a19039d866395e1353be6e98c886: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16996"/><div sID="gen33609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16996"/><hi type="bold">25. when he had supped--</hi>Greek, "after the eating of supper," namely, the Passover supper which preceded the Lord's Supper, as the love-feast did subsequently. Therefore, you Corinthians ought to separate common meals from the Lord's Supper [Bengel].<div eID="gen33609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the new testament--</hi>or "covenant." The cup is the parchment-deed, as it were, on which My new covenant, or last will is written and sealed, making over to you all blessings here and hereafter.<div eID="gen33610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in my blood--</hi>ratified by MY blood: "not by the blood of goats and calves" (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">He 9:12</reference>).<div eID="gen33611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as oft as--</hi>Greek, "as many times soever": implying that it is an ordinance often to be partaken of.<div eID="gen33612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in remembrance of me--</hi>Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.19">Lu 22:19</reference>) expresses this, which is understood by Matthew and Mark. Paul twice records it (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.24">1Co 11:24</reference> and here) as suiting his purpose. The old sacrifices brought sins continually to remembrance (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.1">He 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.3">3</reference>). The Lord's Supper brings to remembrance Christ and His sacrifice once for all for the full and final remission of sins. <div eID="gen33613" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa874c85d62ed3b5b0f026e2a7ced6b83bf03b20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16997"/><div sID="gen33614" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16997"/><hi type="bold">26. For--</hi>in proof that the Lord's Supper is "in remembrance" of Him.<div eID="gen33614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33615" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">show--</hi>announce publicly. The Greek does not mean to dramatically represent, but "ye publicly profess each of you, the Lord has died FOR ME" [Wahl]. This word, as "is" in Christ's institution (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.24">1Co 11:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.25">25</reference>), implies not literal presence, but a vivid realization, by faith, of Christ in the Lord's Supper, as a living person, not a mere abstract dogma, "bone of our bone, and flesh of our flesh" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.30">Ep 5:30</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.2.23">Ge 2:23</reference>); and ourselves "members of His body, of His flesh, and of His bones," "our sinful bodies made clean by His body (once for all offered), and our souls washed through His most precious blood" [Church of England Prayer Book]. "Show," or "announce," is an expression applicable to new things; compare "show" as to the Passover (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.8">Ex 13:8</reference>). So the Lord's death ought always to be fresh in our memory; compare in heaven, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.6">Re 5:6</reference>. That the Lord's Supper is in remembrance of Him, implies that He is bodily absent, though spiritually present, for we cannot be said to commemorate one absent. The fact that we not only show the Lord's death in the supper, but eat and drink the pledges of it, could only be understood by the Jews, accustomed to such feasts after propitiatory sacrifices, as implying our personal appropriation therein of the benefits of that death.<div eID="gen33615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">till he come--</hi>when there shall be no longer need of symbols of His body, the body itself being manifested. The Greek expresses the certainly of His coming. Rome teaches that we eat Christ present corporally, "till He come" corporally; a contradiction in terms. The showbread, literally, "bread of the presence," was in the sanctuary, but not in the Holiest Place (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.1-Heb.9.8">He 9:1-8</reference>); so the Lord's Supper in heaven, the antitype to the Holiest Place, shall be superseded by Christ's own bodily presence; then the wine shall be drunk "anew" in the Father's kingdom, by Christ and His people together, of which heavenly banquet, the Lord's Supper is a spiritual foretaste and specimen (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.29">Mt 26:29</reference>). Meantime, as the showbread was placed anew, every sabbath, on the table before the Lord (<reference osisRef="Lev.24.5-Lev.24.8">Le 24:5-8</reference>); so the Lord's death was shown, or announced afresh at the Lord's table the first day of every week in the primitive Church. We are now "priests unto God" in the dispensation of Christ's spiritual presence, antitypical to the HOLY PLACE: the perfect and eternal dispensation, which shall not begin till Christ's coming, is antitypical to the HOLIEST PLACE, which Christ our High Priest alone in the flesh as yet has entered (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.6">He 9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.7">7</reference>); but which, at His coming, we, too, who are believers, shall enter (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.15">Re 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.22">21:22</reference>). The supper joins the two closing periods of the Old and the New dispensations.
