Let us, therefore, bear it in mind, that this is spoken of Christ as mediator. He is, I say, inferior to the Father, inasmuch as he assumed our nature, <hi type="italic">that he might be the first-born among many brethren.</hi><div eID="gen119017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119018" type="x-p"/>There is somewhat more of difficulty in what follows. Here the man is placed in an intermediate position between Christ and the woman, so that Christ is not the head of the woman. Yet the same Apostle teaches us elsewhere, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.3.28">Galatians 3:28</reference>,) that <hi type="italic">in Christ there is neither male nor female</hi>. Why then does he make a distinction here, which in that passage he does away with? I answer, that the solution of this depends on the connection in which the passages occur. When he says that there is no difference between the man and the woman, he is treating of Christ’s spiritual kingdom, in which individual distinctions <note n="620"> <div sID="gen119019" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Les qualites externes</foreign>;” “External qualities.”<div eID="gen119019" type="x-p"/> </note> are not regarded, or made any account of; for it has nothing to do with the body, and has nothing to do with the outward relationships of mankind, but has to do solely with the mind — on which account he <hi type="italic">declares </hi>that there is no difference, even between <hi type="italic">bond </hi>and <hi type="italic">free</hi>. In the meantime, however, he does not disturb civil order or honorary distinctions, which cannot be dispensed with in ordinary life. Here, on the other hand, he reasons respecting outward propriety and decorum — which is a part of ecclesiastical polity. Hence, as regards spiritual connection in the sight of God, and inwardly in the conscience, Christ is the head of the man and of the woman without any distinction, because, as to that, there is no regard paid to male or female; but as regards external arrangement and political decorum, the man follows Christ and the woman the man, so that they are not upon the same footing, but, on the contrary, this inequality exists. Should any one ask, what connection marriage has with Christ, I answer, that Paul speaks here of that sacred union of pious persons, of which Christ is the officiating priest, <note n="621"> <div sID="gen119020" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Autheur et conducteur</foreign>;” — “Author and conductor.”<div eID="gen119020" type="x-p"/> </note> and He in whose name it is consecrated.<div eID="gen119018" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119013" osisID="1Cor.11.3" type="section"/>
entries.dac4b72cfbd9f82cbdd2c3c5e9938f791c2ef776: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.4" sID="gen119021" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi><hi type="italic"> Every man praying</hi> Here there are two propositions. The first relates to the <hi type="italic">man</hi>, the other to the <hi type="italic">woman</hi> <hi type="italic"> </hi>He says that the <hi type="italic">man </hi>commits an offense against Christ his head, if he <hi type="italic">prays or prophesies with his head covered.</hi> Why so? Because he is subject to Christ, with this understanding, that he is to hold the first place in the government of the house — for the father of the family is like a king in his own house. Hence the glory of God shines forth in him, in consequence of the authority with which he is invested. If he covers his head, he lets himself down from that preeminence which God had assigned to him, so as to be in subjection. Thus the honor of Christ is infringed upon. For example, <note n="622"> <div sID="gen119023" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais afin de mieux entendre ceci, prenons vn exemple</foreign>;” — “But, that we may understand this better, let us take an example.”<div eID="gen119023" type="x-p"/> </note> If the person whom the prince has appointed as his lieutenant, does not know how to maintain his proper station, <note n="623"> <div sID="gen119024" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Se maintenir, et vser de son authorite</foreign>;” — “To keep his place, and maintain his authority.”<div eID="gen119024" type="x-p"/> </note> and instead of this, exposes his dignity to contempt on the part of persons in the lowest station, does he not bring dishonor upon his prince? In like manner, if the <hi type="italic">man </hi>does not keep his own station — if he is not subject to Christ in such a way as to preside over his own family with authority, he obscures, to that extent, the glory of Christ, which shines forth in the well regulated order of marriage. The <hi type="italic">covering</hi>, as we shall see ere long, is an emblem of authority intermediate and interposed.<div eID="gen119022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119025" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Prophesying</hi> I take here to mean — declaring the mysteries of God for the edification of the hearers, (as afterwards in <reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.14.3-1Cor.14.6 Bible:1Cor.14.12 Bible:1Cor.14.16-1Cor.14.17 Bible:1Cor.14.26">1 Corinthians 14</reference>,) as <hi type="italic">praying</hi> means preparing a form of prayer, and taking the lead, as it were, of all the people — which is the part of the public teacher, <note n="624"> <div sID="gen119026" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Du ministre et docteur de l’Eglise</foreign>;” — “Of the minister and teacher of the Church.”<div eID="gen119026" type="x-p"/> </note> for Paul is not arguing here as to every kind of prayer, but as to solemn prayer in public. Let us, however, bear in mind, that in this matter the error is merely in so far as decorum is violated, and the distinction of rank which God has established, is broken in upon. For we must not be so scrupulous as to look upon it as a criminal thing for a teacher to have a cap on his head, when addressing the people from the pulpit. Paul means nothing more than this — that it should appear that the man has authority, and that the woman is under subjection, and this is secured when the man uncovers his head in the view of the Church, though he should afterwards put on his cap again from fear of catching cold. In fine, the <hi type="italic">one </hi>rule to be observed here is <foreign xml:lang="el">το πρέπον</foreign> — <hi type="italic">decorum</hi> If <hi type="italic">that </hi>is secured, Paul requires nothing farther.<div eID="gen119025" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119021" osisID="1Cor.11.4" type="section"/>
entries.9d69b31962134709d759bba8c83f024ab7b942a6: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.5" sID="gen119027" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi><hi type="italic"> Every woman praying or prophesying</hi> Here we have the <hi type="italic">second </hi>proposition — that women ought <hi type="italic">to have their heads covered</hi> when they <hi type="italic">pray</hi> or <hi type="italic">prophesy</hi>; otherwise they <hi type="italic">dishonor their head</hi> For as the <hi type="italic">man</hi> honors his head by showing his liberty, so the <hi type="italic">woman</hi>, by showing her subjection. Hence, on the other hand, if the woman uncovers her head, she shakes off subjection — involving contempt of her husband. It may seem, however, to be superfluous for Paul to forbid the woman to prophesy with her head uncovered, while elsewhere he wholly<div eID="gen119028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119029" type="x-p"/>prohibits women from speaking in the Church. <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Tim.2.12">1 Timothy 2:12</reference>.)<div eID="gen119029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119030" type="x-p"/>It would not, therefore, be allowable for them to prophesy even with a covering upon their head, and hence it follows that it is to no purpose that he argues here as to a covering. It may be replied, that the Apostle, by here condemning the one, does not commend the other. For when he reproves them for prophesying with their head uncovered, he at the same time does not give them permission to prophesy in some other way, but rather delays his condemnation of that vice to another passage, namely in <reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.14.34-1Cor.14.36">1 Corinthians 14</reference>. In this reply there is nothing amiss, though at the same time it might suit sufficiently well to say, that the Apostle requires women to show their modesty — not merely in a place in which the whole Church is assembled, but also in any more dignified assembly, either of matrons or of men, such as are sometimes convened in private houses.<div eID="gen119030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119031" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For it is all one as if she were shaven.</hi> He now maintains from other considerations, that it is unseemly for women to have their heads bare. <hi type="italic">Nature itself</hi>, says he, abhors it. To see a woman shaven is a spectacle that is disgusting and monstrous. Hence we infer that the woman <hi type="italic">has her hair given her for a covering</hi> Should any one now object, that her hair is enough, as being a natural covering, Paul says that it is <hi type="italic">not</hi>, for it is such a covering as requires another thing to be made use of for covering <hi type="italic">it</hi> And hence a conjecture is drawn, with some appearance of probability — that women who had beautiful hair were accustomed to uncover their heads for the purpose of showing off their beauty. It is not, therefore, without good reason that Paul, as a remedy for this vice, sets before them the opposite idea — that they be regarded as remarkable for unseemliness, rather than for what is an incentive to lust. <note n="625"> <div sID="gen119032" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Sainct Paul pour remedier à ce vice, propose tout le contraire de ce qui leur sembloit; disant, que tant s’en faut qu’en cela il y ait vne beaute pour attirer les hommes a connoitise, que plustot c’est vne chose laide et deshonneste</foreign>;” — “St. Paul, with the view of remedying this vice, sets forward quite the reverse of what appeared to them — saying, that so far from there being a beauty in this to allure men to lust, it is rather a thing that is ugly and unseemly.”<div eID="gen119032" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119031" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.5" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119027" osisID="1Cor.11.5" type="section"/>
entries.3a24bd5c90d9dd01388a4f6fddd4a98cdca7337f: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.7" sID="gen119033" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7.</hi> <hi type="italic">The man ought not to cover his head, because he is the image</hi> The same question may now be proposed respecting the <hi type="italic">image</hi>, as formerly respecting the<hi type="italic"> head.</hi> For both sexes were created in the image of God, and Paul exhorts women no less than men to be formed anew, according to that image. The <hi type="italic">image</hi>, however, of which he is now speaking, relates to the order of marriage, and hence it belongs to the present life, and is not connected with conscience. The simple solution is this — that he does not treat here of innocence and holiness, which are equally becoming in men and women, but of the distinction, which God has conferred upon the man, so as to have superiority over the woman. In this superior order of dignity the glory of God is seen, as it shines forth in every kind of superiority.<div eID="gen119034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119035" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The woman is the glory of the man</hi> There is no doubt that the woman is a distinguished ornament of the man; for it is a great honor that God has appointed her to the man as the partner of his life, and a helper to him, <note n="626"> <div sID="gen119036" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour estre compagne a l’homme, pour viure auec luy, et pour luy aider</foreign>;” — “To be a companion to the man, to live with him, and to aid him.”<div eID="gen119036" type="x-p"/> </note> and has made her subject to him as the body is to the head. For what Solomon affirms as to a careful wife — that <hi type="italic">she is a crown to her husband</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Prov.12.4">Proverbs 12:4</reference>,) is true of the whole sex, if we look to the appointment of God, which Paul here commends, showing that the woman was created for this purpose — that she might be a distinguished ornament of the man.<div eID="gen119035" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119033" osisID="1Cor.11.7" type="section"/>
entries.f3e0f32f5003b37f519af10229fd2110a08e9615: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.8" sID="gen119037" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> <hi type="italic">For the man is not from the woman.</hi> He establishes by <hi type="italic">two </hi>arguments the pre-eminence, which he had assigned to men above women. The <hi type="italic">first </hi>is, that as the woman derives her origin from the man, she is therefore inferior in rank. The <hi type="italic">second </hi>is, that as the woman was created for the sake of the man, she is therefore subject to him, as the work ultimately produced is to its cause. <note n="627"> <div sID="gen119039" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ainsi que l’oeuure tendant a quelque fin est au dessous de sa cause et fin pour laquelle on le fait</foreign>;” — “As a work fitted for some design is inferior to its cause and the design for which it is made.”<div eID="gen119039" type="x-p"/> </note> That the man is the beginning of the woman and the end for which she was made, is evident from the law. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.2.18">Genesis 2:18</reference>.)<div eID="gen119038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119040" type="x-p"/>It is not good for a man to be alone. Let us make for him, etc.<div eID="gen119040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119041" type="x-p"/>Farther,<div eID="gen119041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119042" type="x-p"/>God took one of Adam’s ribs and formed Eve. <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.2.21 Bible:Gen.2.22">Genesis 2:21, 22</reference>.)<div eID="gen119042" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119037" osisID="1Cor.11.8" type="section"/>
entries.abd8ce09118fca08f8499d2f9ed64e5c27f4f7c3: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.10" sID="gen119043" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi><hi type="italic"> For this cause ought the woman to have power</hi> <note n="628"> <div sID="gen119045" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Doit auoir sur la teste vne enseigne qu’elle est sous puissance</foreign>;” — “She ought to have upon her head a token that she is under authority.”<div eID="gen119045" type="x-p"/> </note> From that authority he draws an argument <note n="629"> <div sID="gen119046" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vn argument et consequence</foreign>;” — “An argument and inference.”<div eID="gen119046" type="x-p"/> </note> in favor of outward decorum. “She is subject,” says he, “let her then wear a token of subjection.” In the term <hi type="italic">power</hi>, there is an instance of metonymy, <note n="630"> <div sID="gen119047" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">I1 y a de mot a mot au Grec, La femme doit auoir puissance sur la teste. Mais au mot de <hi type="italic">puissance </hi>il y a une figure appellee metonymie</foreign>;” — “It is literally in the Greek, The woman ought to have power upon her head. But in the word <hi type="italic">power </hi>there is a figure called metonymy.”<div eID="gen119047" type="x-p"/> </note> for he means a token by which she declares herself to be under the power of her husband; and it is a covering, whether it be a robe, or a veil, <note n="631"> <div sID="gen119048" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est la couuerture de teste, soit un chapperon, ou couurechef, ou coiffe, ou chose semblable</foreign>;” — “It is a covering of the head, whether it be a hood, or a kerchief, or a coif, or anything of that kind.”<div eID="gen119048" type="x-p"/> </note> or any other kind of covering. <note n="632"> <div sID="gen119049" type="x-p"/> The term <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐξουσία</foreign> (<hi type="italic">exousia</hi>) is considered by Bloomfield to be the <hi type="italic">name </hi>of an article of dress of which mention is made in <reference osisRef="Bible:Ruth.3.15">Ruth 3:15</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.23">Isaiah 3:23</reference>, and consisted of “a piece of cloth of a square form thrown over the head and tied under the chin.” Granville Penn, on the other hand, considers it as nothing more than the (<foreign xml:lang="el">τι</foreign>) <foreign xml:lang="el">κατα κεφαλης</foreign> in the third verse of the <hi type="italic">chapter</hi> — <hi type="italic">something on the head</hi>, or a <hi type="italic">covering on the head</hi>, and notices it as remarkable, that in Wiclif’s version (1380) the rendering is — “the woman schal have an <hi type="italic">hilying </hi>on hir heed,” which the glossary explains by <hi type="italic">covering</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen119049" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119050" type="x-p"/>It is asked, whether he speaks of <hi type="italic">married </hi>women exclusively, for there are some that restrict to <hi type="italic">them </hi>what Paul here teaches, on the ground that it does not belong to virgins to be under the authority of a husband. It is however a mistake, for Paul looks beyond this — to God’s eternal law, which has made the female sex subject to the authority of men. On this account all women are born, that they may acknowledge themselves inferior in consequence of the superiority of the male sex. Otherwise it were an inconclusive argument that Paul has drawn from <hi type="italic">nature</hi>, in saying that it were not one whit more seemly for a woman to <hi type="italic">have her head uncovered</hi> than to be <hi type="italic">shaven</hi> — this being applicable to virgins also.<div eID="gen119050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119051" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Because of the angels</hi> This passage is explained in various ways. As the Prophet <reference osisRef="Bible:Mal.2.7">Malachi 2:7</reference> calls priests <hi type="italic">angels of God</hi>,<hi type="italic"> </hi>some are of opinion that Paul speaks of <hi type="italic">them</hi>; but the ministers of the word have nowhere that term applied to them by itself — that is, without something being added; and the meaning would be too forced. I understand it, therefore, in its proper signification. But it is asked, why it is that he would have women have their heads covered <hi type="italic">because of the angels</hi> — for what has this to do with them? Some answer: “Because they are present on occasion of the prayers of believers, and on this account are spectators of unseemliness, should there be any on such occasions.” But what need is there for philosophizing with such refinement? We know that angels are in attendance, also, upon Christ as their head, and minister to him. <note n="633"> <div sID="gen119052" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et sont tousiours a son commandement et seruice</foreign>;” — “And are always at his commandment and service.”<div eID="gen119052" type="x-p"/> </note> When, therefore, women venture upon such liberties, as to usurp for themselves the token of authority, they make their baseness manifest to the angels. This, therefore, was said by way of amplifying, as if he had said, “If women uncover their heads, not only Christ, but all the angels too, will be witnesses of the outrage.” And this interpretation suits well with the Apostle’s design. He is treating here of different ranks. Now he says that, when women assume a higher place than becomes them, they gain this by it — that they discover their impudence in the view of the angels of heaven.<div eID="gen119051" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119043" osisID="1Cor.11.10" type="section"/>
entries.d712c53f1fd578983d3b53fd2752a8dcd7379af4: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.11" sID="gen119053" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> <hi type="italic">But neither is the man without the woman</hi> This is added partly as a check upon men, that they may not insult over women; <note n="634"> <div sID="gen119055" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qu’ils n’ayent les femmes en desdain et mocquerie</foreign>;” — “That they may not hold women in disdain and derision.”<div eID="gen119055" type="x-p"/> </note> and partly as a consolation to women, that they may not feel dissatisfied with being under subjection. “The male sex (says he) has a distinction over the female sex, with this understanding, that they ought to be connected together by mutual benevolence, for the one cannot do without the other. If they be separated, they are like the mutilated members of a mangled body. Let them, therefore, be connected with each other by the bond of mutual duty.” <note n="635"> <div sID="gen119056" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par ce lien d’aide et antitie mutuelle</foreign>;” — “By this tie of mutual assistance and amity.”<div eID="gen119056" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119057" type="x-p"/>When he says, <hi type="italic">in the Lord</hi>, he by this expression calls the attention of believers to the appointment of the Lord, while the wicked look to nothing beyond pressing necessity. <note n="636"> <div sID="gen119058" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La necessite qui les presse et contraint</foreign>;” — “The necessity that presses and constrains them.”<div eID="gen119058" type="x-p"/> </note> For profane men, if they can conveniently live unmarried, despise the whole sex, and do not consider that they are under obligations to it by the appointment and decree of God. The pious, on the other hand, acknowledge that the male sex is but the half of the human race. They ponder the meaning of that statement — <hi type="italic">God created man</hi>:<hi type="italic"> male and female created he them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.27">Genesis 1:27</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.5.2">Genesis 5:2</reference>.) Thus they, of their own accord, acknowledge themselves to be debtors to the weaker sex. Pious women, in like manner, reflect upon their obligation. <note n="637"> <div sID="gen119059" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pensent a leur deuoir, et que de leur coste elles sont obligees aux hommes</foreign>;” — “Think of their duty, and of their being under obligation, on their part, to men.”<div eID="gen119059" type="x-p"/> </note> Thus the man has no standing without the woman, for that would be the head severed from the body; nor has the woman without the man, for that were a body without a head. “Let, therefore, the man perform to the woman the office of the head in respect of ruling her, and let the woman perform to the man the office of the body in respect of assisting him, and that not merely in the married state, but also in celibacy; for I do not speak of cohabitation merely, but also of civil offices, for which there is occasion even in the unmarried state.” If you are inclined rather to refer this to the whole sex in general, I do not object to this, though, as Paul directs his discourse to individuals, he appears to point out the particular duty of each.<div eID="gen119057" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119053" osisID="1Cor.11.11" type="section"/>
entries.37b305151794806d15e4f13f2eebf2120cf0483b: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.12" sID="gen119060" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> <hi type="italic">As the woman is of the man</hi> If this is one of the reasons, why the man has superiority — that the woman was taken out of him, there will be, in like manner, this motive to friendly connection — that the male sex cannot maintain and preserve itself without the aid of women. For this remains a settled point — that <hi type="italic">it is not good for man to be alone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.2.18">Genesis 2:18</reference>.) This statement of Paul may, it is true, be viewed as referring to propagation, because human beings are propagated not by men alone, but by men and women; but I understand it as meaning this also — that the woman is a needful help to the man, inasmuch as a solitary life is not expedient for man. This decree of God exhorts us to cultivate mutual intercourse.<div eID="gen119061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119062" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">But all things of God</hi> God is the Source of both sexes, and hence both of them ought with humility to accept and maintain the condition which the Lord has assigned to them. Let the <hi type="italic">man</hi> exercise his authority with moderation, and not insult over the woman who has been given him as his partner. Let the <hi type="italic">woman</hi> be satisfied with her state of subjection, and not take it amiss that she is made inferior to the more distinguished sex. Otherwise they will both of them throw off the yoke of God, who has not without good reason appointed this distinction of ranks. Farther, when it is said that the man and the woman, when they are wanting in their duty to each other, are rebels against the authority of God, the statement is a more serious one than if Paul had said, that they do injury to one another.<div eID="gen119062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119063" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Doth not even nature itself</hi> He again sets forth <hi type="italic">nature </hi>as the mistress of decorum, and what was at that time in common use by universal consent and custom — even among the Greeks — he speaks of as being <hi type="italic">natural</hi>, for it was not always reckoned a disgrace for men to have long hair. <note n="638"> <div sID="gen119064" type="x-p"/> It is remarked by President Edwards, that “the emphasis used, <foreign xml:lang="el">αὐτὴ ἡ φύσις</foreign>, <hi type="italic">nature itself</hi>, shows that the Apostle does not mean custom, but nature in the proper sense. It is true it was long custom that made having the head covered a token of subjection, and a feminine habit or appearance, as it is custom that makes any outward action or word a sign or signification of anything; but nature itself, nature in its proper sense, teaches that it is a shame for a man to appear with the established signs of the female sex. Nature itself shows it to be a shame for a father to bow down or kneel to his own child or servant, because bowing down is, by custom, an established token of subjection and submission.” Edwards on Original Sin, part 2, chapter 3, section 3. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen119064" type="x-p"/> </note> Historical records bear, that in all countries in ancient times, that is, in the first ages, men wore long hair. Hence also the poets, in speaking of the ancients, are accustomed to apply to them the common epithet of <hi type="italic">unshorn</hi> <note n="639"> <div sID="gen119065" type="x-p"/> Instances of this occur in Ovid, Fast. 2. 30, and in Hor., Od. 2, 15, 11. Gaul, to the north of the Alps, was called Gallia <hi type="italic">comata</hi>, from the inhabitants <hi type="italic">wearing their hair long</hi> Homer applies to the Greeks in his time the epithet of <foreign xml:lang="el">καρηκομόωντες</foreign> — <hi type="italic">long-haired</hi> Hom. Il., 2. 11. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen119065" type="x-p"/> </note> It was not until a late period that barbers began to be employed at Rome — about the time of Africanus the elder. And at the time when Paul wrote these things, the practice of having the hair shorn had not yet come into use in the provinces of Gaul or in Germany. Nay more, it would have been reckoned an unseemly thing for men, no less than for women, to be shorn or shaven; but as in Greece it was reckoned all unbecoming thing for a man to allow his hair to grow long, so that those who did so were remarked as effeminate, he reckons as <hi type="italic">nature </hi>a custom that had come to be confirmed. <note n="640"> <div sID="gen119066" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">I1 appelle Nature ceste coustume desia confermee par vn long temps et vsage commun</foreign>;” — “He gives the appellation of Nature to this custom, already confirmed by length of time and common use.”<div eID="gen119066" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119063" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119060" osisID="1Cor.11.12" type="section"/>

16. But if any man seem A contentious person is one whose humor inclines him to stir up disputes, and does not care what becomes of the truth. Of this description are all who, without any necessity, abolish good and useful customs — raise disputes respecting matters that are not doubtful — who do not yield to reasonings — who cannot endure that any one should be above them. Of this description, also, are those (ἀκοινώνητοι) would be singular persons
“Qui ne se veulent en rien accommoder aux autres;” — “Who are not disposed to accommodate themselves to others in anything.” — The Greek word made use of by Calvin here (ακοινωντος) is employed by classical writers to mean — having no intercourse, or not caring to have intercourse with others. See Arist., Top. 3. 2, 8.; Plat. Legg., 774 A. — Ed
who, from a foolish affectation,
“Et appetit sans raison;” — “And unreasonable desire.”
aim at some new and unusual way of acting. Such persons Paul does not reckon worthy of being replied to, inasmuch as contention is a pernicious thing, and ought, therefore, to be banished from the Churches. By this he teaches us, that those that are obstinate and fond of quarrelling, should rather be restrained by authority than confuted by lengthened disputations. For you will never have an end of contentions, if you are disposed to contend with a combative person until you have vanquished him; for though vanquished a hundred times, he would argue still. Let us therefore carefully mark this passage, that we may not allow ourselves to be carried away with needless disputations, provided at the same time we know how to distinguish contentious persons. For we must not always reckon as contentious the man who does not acquiesce in our decisions, or who ventures to contradict us; but when temper and obstinacy show themselves, let us then say with Paul, that contentions are at variance with the custom of the Church
“Que ce n’est point la coustume de l’Eglise d’entrer en debats et contentions;” — “That it is not the custom of the Church to enter into strifes and contentions.”
1 Corinthians 11:17-22
17. Now in this that I declare unto you I praise you not, that ye come together not for the better, but for the worse.
17. Hoc autem denuntians non laudo, quod non in melius, sed in peius convenitis.
18. For first of all, when ye come together in the church, I hear that there be divisions among you; and I partly believe it.
18. Primum enim, convenientibus vobis in Ecclesiam, audio dissidia inter vos esse: et ex parte credo.
19. For there must be also heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you.
19. Oportet enim haereses quoque esse in vobis, ut qui probe sunt, manifesti fiant inter vos.
20. When ye come together therefore into one place, this is not to eat the Lord’s supper.
20. Convenientibus ergo vobis in unum, non est Dominicam coenamedere.
21. For in eating every one taketh before other his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken.
21. Unusquisque enim propriam coenam praesumit edendo: atque hic quidem esurit, ille autem ebrius est.
22. What? have ye not houses to eat and to drink in? or despise ye the church of God, and shame them that have not? What shall I say to you? shall I praise you in this? I praise you not.
22. Numquid domos non habetis, ad edendum et bibendum, aut Ecclesiam Dei contemnitis, et pudore afficitis eos qui non habent? Quid vobis dicam? Laudabo vos in hoc? Non laudo.
entries.db9d68a67a9448cd6538777a82650c8f401f9119: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.17" sID="gen119087" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119088" type="x-p"/>His reproof of the fault previously noticed was but a mild and gentle admonition, because the Corinthians sinned in ignorance, so that it was proper that they should readily be forgiven. Paul, too, had praised them in the outset, because they had faithfully <hi type="italic">kept his enactments</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.11.2">1 Corinthians 11:2</reference>.) Now he begins to reprove them more sharply, because they offended more grievously in some things, and not through ignorance.<div eID="gen119088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119089" type="x-p"/>17. <hi type="italic">But, in warning you as to this, I do not praise.</hi> <note n="644"> <div sID="gen119090" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">Or ie vous rememore ceci</hi>,<hi type="italic"> non point eu louant</hi>. I1 y a au Grec mot; a mot. Or rememorant ie ne loue point</foreign>;” — “<hi type="italic">But I put you in</hi>,<hi type="italic"> mind of this</hi>,<hi type="italic"> not praising you for it</hi>. It is literally in the Greek: But putting you in mind I do not praise.”<div eID="gen119090" type="x-p"/> </note> For I translate it in this way, because Paul appears to have made the participle and the verb change places. <note n="645"> <div sID="gen119091" type="x-p"/> In explanation of this remark, let it be observed that the reading in the Alexandrine MS. is as follows: <foreign xml:lang="el">Τοῦτο δε παραγγέλλω οὐκ ἐπαινῶν</foreign> — But I warn you as to this, not praising. This reading is followed in the Latin and Syrian versions. In Wiclif (1380) the rendering is: “But this thing I comaunde, not preisynge.” In Rheims (1582) — “And this I commaund; not praising it.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen119091" type="x-p"/> </note> I am also not satisfied with the interpretation of Erasmus, who takes <foreign xml:lang="el">παραγγέλλειν</foreign> as meaning to <hi type="italic">command</hi> The verb to <hi type="italic">warn </hi>would suit better, but as to this I do not contend. There is an antithesis between this clause and the beginning of this chapter. “While I have praised you, do not think that it is unqualified commendation; for I have something to find fault with, as it is worthy of severe reproof.” This, however, in my opinion, does not refer exclusively to the Lord’s Supper, but also to other faults of which he makes mention. Let this then be taken as a general statement, that the Corinthians are reproved, because they <hi type="italic">came together not for the better but for the worse.</hi> Particular effects of this evil will be brought forward afterwards.<div eID="gen119089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119092" type="x-p"/>He finds fault with them, then, in the <hi type="italic">first </hi>place, because they <hi type="italic">come not together for the better</hi>, — and<hi type="italic"> secondly</hi>, that they <hi type="italic">come together for the worse</hi> The <hi type="italic">second</hi>, it is true, is the more serious, but even the <hi type="italic">first </hi>is not to be endured, for if we consider what is transacted in the Church, there ought never to be a <hi type="italic">coming together</hi> without some fruit. <hi type="italic">There</hi> the doctrine of God is listened to, prayers are offered up, the Sacraments are administered. The fruit of the Word is, when confidence in God and fear of him are increased in us — when progress is made in holiness of life — when we put off more and more the <hi type="italic">old man</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.3.9">Colossians 3:9</reference>) — when we advance in <hi type="italic">newness of life</hi>, etc. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.4">Romans 6:4</reference>.) The Sacraments have a tendency to exercise us in piety and love. The prayers, too, ought to be of use for promoting all these purposes. In addition to this, the Lord works efficaciously by his Spirit, because he wills not that his ordinances should be vain. Hence if the sacred assemblies are of no benefit to us, and we are not made better by them, it is our ingratitude that is to blame, and therefore we deserve to be reproved. For the effect of our conduct is, that those things, which, from their own nature, and from God’s appointment, ought to have been salutary, become unprofitable.<div eID="gen119092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119093" type="x-p"/>Then follows the <hi type="italic">second </hi>fault — that they <hi type="italic">come together for the worse.</hi> This is much more criminal, and yet it almost always follows the other, for if we derive no advantage from God’s benefits, he employs this method of punishing our carelessness — that we are <hi type="italic">made worse</hi> by them. It usually happens, too, that negligence gives birth to many corruptions, especially on this account, that those who do not observe the natural use of things usually fall erelong into hurtful inventions. <note n="646"> <div sID="gen119094" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Principalement pource que ceux qui ne regardent pas a tenir le droit et naturel usage des choses, sont suiets a tomber incontinent en beaucoup d’inuentions peruerses et dangereuses</foreign>;” — “Chiefly because those who do not take care to observe the right and natural use of things, are liable to fall straightway into many perverse and dangerous inventions.”<div eID="gen119094" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119093" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119087" osisID="1Cor.11.17" type="section"/>
entries.262785709b267e32a23b78807eabbbb389919d4d: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.18" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.18" sID="gen119095" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18.</hi><hi type="italic"> When ye come together in the Church, I hear there are divisions</hi> Some take the words <hi type="italic">divisions</hi> and <hi type="italic">heresies</hi>, as referring to that disorder (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἀταξίαν</foreign>) of which he speaks soon afterwards. I consider them as having a more extensive signification, and certainly it is not likely that he would employ terms so improper and unsuitable for the purpose of exposing that abuse. <note n="647"> <div sID="gen119097" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qu’il leur remonstrera qu’ils fout en la Cene</foreign>;” — “Which he will show that they have fallen into as to the Supper.”<div eID="gen119097" type="x-p"/> </note> For as to their alleging that he has expressed himself in more severe terms, with the view of exposing more fully the heinousness of the offense, I would readily grant this, if the meaning corresponded. It is, then, a reproof of a general kind — that they were not of one accord as becomes Christians, but every one was so much taken up with his own interests, that he was not prepared to accommodate himself to others. Hence arose that abuse, as to which we shall see in a little — hence sprung ambition and pride, so that every one exalted himself and despised others — hence sprung carelessness as to edification — hence sprung profanation of the gifts of God.<div eID="gen119096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119098" type="x-p"/>He says that he <hi type="italic">partly believes it</hi>, that they might not think that he charged them all with this heinous crime, and might accordingly complain, that they were groundlessly accused. In the meantime, however, he intimates that this had been brought to him not by mere vague rumor, but by credible information, such as he could not altogether discredit.<div eID="gen119098" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.18" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119095" osisID="1Cor.11.18" type="section"/>
entries.5b16470639331456e79c55193799a006c50cd3be: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.19" sID="gen119099" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19.</hi> <hi type="italic">For there must be also heresies</hi> He had previously spoken of <hi type="italic">divisions</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.11.18">1 Corinthians 11:18</reference>.) Now he uses the term <hi type="italic">heresies</hi>, with the view of amplifying the more, as we may infer, too, from the word <hi type="italic">also</hi>, for it is added for the sake of amplification. (<foreign xml:lang="el">προς αὔξησιν</foreign>.) It is well known in what sense the ancients used those two terms, <note n="648"> <div sID="gen119101" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Schisme et Heresie</foreign>;” — “Schism and Heresy.”<div eID="gen119101" type="x-p"/> </note> and what distinction they made between Heretics and Schismatics. <note n="649"> <div sID="gen119102" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Voyez l’Institution</foreign>;” — “See my Institutes,” (volume 3.)<div eID="gen119102" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">Heresy </hi>they made to consist in disagreement as to doctrine, and <hi type="italic">schism</hi>, on the contrary, in alienation of affection, as when any one withdrew from the Church from envy, or from dislike of the pastors, or from ill nature. It is true, that the Church cannot but be torn asunder by false doctrine, and thus heresy is the root and origin of schism, and it is also true that envy or pride is the mother of almost all heresies, but at the same time it is of advantage to distinguish in this way between these two terms.<div eID="gen119100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119103" type="x-p"/>But let us see in what sense Paul employs them. I have already expressed my disapprobation of those who explain heresy as meaning the setting up of a separate table, inasmuch as the rich did not partake of their Supper along with the poor; for he had it in view to point out something more hateful. But without mentioning the opinions of others, I take <hi type="italic">schism </hi>and <hi type="italic">heresy </hi>here in the way of less and greater. Schisms, then, are either secret grudges — when we do not see that agreement which ought to subsist among the pious — when inclinations at variance with each other are at work — when every one is mightily pleased with his own way, and finds fault with everything that is done by others. <hi type="italic">Heresies</hi> are when the evil proceeds to such a pitch that open hostility is discovered, and persons deliberately divide themselves into opposite parties. Hence, in order that believers might not feel discouraged on seeing the Corinthians torn with <hi type="italic">divisions</hi>, the Apostle turns round this occasion of offense in an opposite direction, intimating that the Lord does rather by such trials make proof of his people’s constancy. A lovely consolation! “So far, says he, should we be from being troubled, or cast down, when we do not see complete unity in the Church, but on the contrary some threatenings of separation from want of proper agreement, that even if sects should start up, <note n="650"> <div sID="gen119104" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De tous costez</foreign>;” — “On all sides.”<div eID="gen119104" type="x-p"/> </note> we ought to remain firm and constant. For in this way hypocrites are detected — in this way, on the other hand, the sincerity of believers is tried. For as this gives occasion for discovering the fickleness of those who were not rooted in the Lord’s Word, and the wickedness of those who had assumed the appearance of good men, so the good afford a more signal manifestation of their constancy and sincerity.”<div eID="gen119103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119105" type="x-p"/>But observe what Paul says — <hi type="italic">there must be,</hi> for he intimates by this expression, that this state of matters does not happen by chance, but by the sure providence of God, because he has it in view to try his people, as gold in the furnace, and if it is agreeable to the mind of God, it is, consequently, expedient. At the same time, however, we must not enter into thorny disputes, or rather into labyrinths as to a fatal necessity. We know that there never will be a time when there will not be many reprobates. We know that they are governed by the spirit of Satan, and are effectually drawn away to what is evil. We know that Satan, in his activity, leaves no stone unturned with the view of breaking up the unity of the Church. From this — not from fate — comes that necessity of which Paul makes mention. <note n="651"> <div sID="gen119106" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De la vient ceste necessite de laquelle S. Paul fait mention, et non pas de ce Fatum que les Stoiques ont imagine, que l’on nomme communeement Destinee. Voyez l’ Institution</foreign>;” — “From this comes that necessity of which St. Paul makes mention, and not from that Fate of which the Stoics have dreamed, and which is commonly called destiny. See the Institutes.” (Volume 1, p. 241.)<div eID="gen119106" type="x-p"/> </note> We know, also, that the Lord, by his admirable wisdom, turns Satan’s deadly machinations so as to promote the salvation of believers. <note n="652"> <div sID="gen119107" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Conuertit au profit et salut des fideles les machinations de Satan horribles et pernicieuses</foreign>;” — “Turns the horrible and pernicious machinations of Satan to the advantage and salvation of believers.”<div eID="gen119107" type="x-p"/> </note> Hence comes that design of which he speaks — <hi type="italic">that the good may shine forth more conspicuously</hi>; for we ought not to ascribe this advantage to <hi type="italic">heresies</hi>, which, being evil, can produce nothing but what is evil, but to God, who, by his infinite goodness, changes the nature of things, so that those things are salutary to the elect, which Satan had contrived for their ruin. As to Chrysostom’s contending that the particle <hi type="italic">that </hi>(<foreign xml:lang="el">ἴνα</foreign>) denotes not the cause, but the event, it is of no great moment. For the cause is the secret counsel of God, <note n="653"> <div sID="gen119108" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Car a parlet proprement, la cause de ceci depend du secret conseil de Dieu</foreign>;” — “For, properly speaking, the cause of this depends on the secret counsel of God.”<div eID="gen119108" type="x-p"/> </note> by which things that are evil are overruled in such a manner, as to have a good issue. We know, in fine, that the wicked are impelled by Satan in such a manner, that they both act and are acted upon with the consent of their wills. <note n="654"> <div sID="gen119109" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ce qu’ils font, et ce que Satan lear fait faire, ils le font volontairement, et non point par force</foreign>;” — “What they do, and what Satan makes them do, they do voluntarily, and not from force.”<div eID="gen119109" type="x-p"/> </note> Hence they are without excuse.<div eID="gen119105" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119099" osisID="1Cor.11.19" type="section"/>
entries.c72333dba2465c36a45fa84218905f275887fef8: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.20" sID="gen119110" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20.</hi> <hi type="italic">This is not to eat the Lord’s supper</hi> He now reproves the abuse that had crept in among the Corinthians as to the Lord’s Supper, in respect of their mixing up profane banquets with the sacred and spiritual feast, and that too with contempt of the poor. Paul says, that in this way it is not <hi type="italic">the Lord’s supper</hi> that is partaken of — not that a single abuse altogether set aside the sacred institution of Christ, and reduced it to nothing, but that they polluted the sacrament by observing it in a wrong way. For we are accustomed to say, in common conversation, that a thing is not done at all, if it is not done aright. Now this was no trivial abuse, as we shall afterwards see. If you understand the words <hi type="italic">is not</hi> as meaning, <hi type="italic">is not allowable</hi>, <note n="655"> <div sID="gen119112" type="x-p"/> Paraeus and some others take the words <foreign xml:lang="el">ὀυκ ἔστι</foreign> <hi type="italic">is not</hi>, as used for, <foreign xml:lang="el">ουκ ἔξεστι</foreign><hi type="italic"> is not allowable</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen119112" type="x-p"/> </note> the meaning will amount to the same thing — that the Corinthians were not in a state of preparation for partaking of <hi type="italic">the Lord’s</hi> supper, as being in so divided a state. What I stated a little ago, however, is more simple — that he condemns that profane admixture, which had nothing in it akin to the Lord’s Supper.<div eID="gen119111" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119110" osisID="1Cor.11.20" type="section"/>
entries.6c0fd9d0b5e5e727e8faa3fbd2384a2216a5fe45: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.21" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.21" sID="gen119113" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21.</hi> <hi type="italic">For every one of you taketh before others his own supper.</hi> It is truly wonderful, and next to a miracle, <note n="656"> <div sID="gen119115" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Quasi incroyable</foreign>;” — “As it were incredible.”<div eID="gen119115" type="x-p"/> </note> that Satan could have accomplished so much in so short a time. We are, however, admonished by this instance, how much antiquity, without reason on its side, can effect, or, in other words, how much influence a long continued custom has, while not sanctioned by a single declaration of the word of God. This, having become customary, was looked upon as lawful. Paul was then at hand to interfere. What then must have been the state of matters after the death of the Apostles? With what liberty Satan must have sported himself. <note n="657"> <div sID="gen119116" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">A ioue ses tours</foreign>;” — “Have played off his tricks.”<div eID="gen119116" type="x-p"/> </note> Yet here is the great strength of Papists: “The thing is ancient — it was done long ago — let it, therefore, have the weight of a revelation from heaven.”<div eID="gen119114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119117" type="x-p"/>It is uncertain, however, what was the origin of this abuse, or what was the occasion of its springing up so soon. Chrysostom is of opinion, that it originated in the love-feasts, <note n="658"> <div sID="gen119118" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vne sorte de banquets qui se faisoyent par charite</foreign>;” — “A kind of banquets that were held, by way of love.”<div eID="gen119118" type="x-p"/> </note> (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἀπὸ τῶν ἀγαπῶν</foreign>) and that, while the rich had been accustomed <note n="659"> <div sID="gen119119" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Premierement</foreign>;” — “At first.”<div eID="gen119119" type="x-p"/> </note> to bring with them from their houses the means of feasting with the poor indiscriminately and in common, they afterwards began to exclude the poor, and to guzzle over their delicacies by themselves. And, certainly, it appears from Tertullian, that that custom was a very ancient one. <note n="660"> <div sID="gen119120" type="x-p"/> Pliny is supposed to refer to the <foreign xml:lang="el">Αγαπὰι</foreign> (<hi type="italic">love-feasts</hi>) in his 97th letter to Trajan, where he says of the Christians in Blthynia, of which he was governor, that, upon examination, they affirmed, that after having taken their <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">sacramenturn</hi></foreign> — “<foreign xml:lang="la">morem sibi discedendi fuisse, rursusque coeundi ad capiendum cibum, promiscuum tamen et innoxium</foreign>;” — “it was customary for them to depart, and come together again for the purpose of taking an innocent repast in common.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen119120" type="x-p"/> </note> Now they gave the name of <hi type="italic">Agapae</hi> <note n="661"> <div sID="gen119121" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">Agapas</hi>, c’est a dire Charitez</foreign>;” — “<hi type="italic">Agapae</hi>, that is to say — Loves.”<div eID="gen119121" type="x-p"/> </note> to those common entertainments, which they contrived among themselves, as being tokens of fraternal affection, and consisted of alms. Nor have I any doubt, that it took its rise from sacrificial rites commonly observed both by Jews and Gentiles. For I observe that Christians, for the most part, corrected the faults connected with those rites, in such a manner, as to retain at the same time some resemblance. Hence it is probable, that, on observing that both Jews and Gentiles added a feast to their sacrifice, as an appendage to it, but that both of them sinned in respect of ambition, luxury, and intemperance, they instituted <note n="662"> <div sID="gen119122" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par succession de temps</foreign>;” — “In process of time.”<div eID="gen119122" type="x-p"/> </note> a kind of banquet, which might accustom them rather to sobriety and frugality, <note n="663"> <div sID="gen119123" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">Qu</hi>’<hi type="italic">autrement</hi></foreign>;” — “Than otherwise.”<div eID="gen119123" type="x-p"/> </note> and might, at the same time, be in accordance with a spiritual entertainment in respect of mutual fellowship. For in it the poor were entertained at the expense of the rich, and the table was open to all. But, whether they had from the very first fallen into this profane abuse, or whether an institution, otherwise not so objectionable, had in this way degenerated in process of time, Paul would have them in no way mix up this spiritual banquet with common feasts. “This, indeed, looks well — that the poor along with the rich partake in common of the provisions that have been brought, and that the rich share of their abundance along with the needy, but nothing ought to have such weight with us as to lead us to profane the holy sacrament.” <note n="664"> <div sID="gen119124" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic"> “</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais il n’y a consideration aucune qui nous doyue tant esmouuoir, que pour cela nous venions a profaner ce sainct mystere</foreign>;” — “But there is no consideration that should have so much influence over us, that we should come, on that account, to profane this holy sacrament.”<div eID="gen119124" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119125" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And one is hungry</hi> This was one evil in the case, that while the rich indulged themselves sumptuously, they appeared, in a manner, to reproach the poor for their poverty. The inequality he describes hyperbolically, when he says, that some are <hi type="italic">drunken </hi>and others are <hi type="italic">hungry</hi>, for some had the means of stuffing themselves well, while others had slender fare. Thus the poor were exposed to the derision of the rich, or at least they were exposed to shame. It was, therefore, an unseemly spectacle, and not in accordance with the <hi type="italic">Lord</hi>’<hi type="italic">s supper</hi><div eID="gen119125" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119113" osisID="1Cor.11.21" type="section"/>
entries.db21cee10d99e7bbefc28382654e96d24f112b22:
22. Have ye not houses? From this we see that the Apostle was utterly dissatisfied with this custom of feasting, even though the abuse formerly mentioned had not existed. For, though it seems allowable for the whole Church to partake at one common table, yet this, on the other hand, is wrong — to convert a sacred assembly to purposes foreign to its nature. We know for what exercises a Church should assemble — to hear doctrine, to pour forth prayers, and sing hymns to God, to observe the sacraments,
“Pour receuoir et administrer los sacrements;” — “To receive and administer the sacraments.”
to make confession of their faith, and to engage in pious observances, and other exercises of piety. If anything else is done there, it is out of place. Every one has his own house appointed him for eating and drinking, and hence that is an unseemly thing in a sacred assembly.
What shall I say to you? Having fitly stated the case, he now calls them to consider, whether they are worthy to be praised, for they could not defend an abuse that was so manifest. He presses them still further, by asking — “What else could I do? Will you say that you are unjustly reproved?” Some manuscripts connect the words in this with the verb that follows — in this way: Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you
The earlier English versions follow this reading. Thus Wiclif, (1380) — What schal I seie to zou? I preise zou: but hereynne I preise zou not; Tyndale, (1534) — What shall I saye unto you? Shall I prayse you: In this prayse I you not; Cranmer, (1539) — What shall I saye unto you? Shall I prayse you? In this prayse I you, not. — Ed.
The other reading, however, is the more generally received among the Greeks, and it suits better.
1 Corinthians 11:23-29
23. For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread:
23. Ego enim accepi a Domino, quod etiam tradidi vobis: quod Dominus Iesus nocte qua traditus est, accepit panem:
24. And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
24. Et gratiis actis, fregit, et dixit, Accipite, edite: hoc est corpus meum quod pro vobis frangitur: hoc facite in mei memoriam.
25. After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.
25. Similiter et calicem, postquam vum testamentum est in sanguine meo: hoc facite, quotiescunque biberitis, in mei memoriam.
26. For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come.
26. Quotiescumque enim ederitis panem hunc, et biberitis hunc calicem, mortem Domini annuntiabitis, donce veniat.
27. Wherefore, whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.
27. Itaque quisquis ederit panem hunc, aut biberit calicem Domini indigne, reus erit corporis et sanguinis Domini.
28. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
28. Probet autem homo se ipsum, et sic de pane illo edat, et de calice bibat.
29. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.
29. Qui enim ederit aut biberit indigne, iudicium sibi edit ac bibit, non discernens corpus Domini.
entries.b850c72e177d1eef2d0ef03cca6ab76b78d3b59c:
Hitherto he has been exposing the abuse;
“Qu’ils commettoyent en la Cene;” — “Which they had fallen into as to the Supper.”
now he proceeds to show what is the proper method of rectifying it. For the institution of Christ is a sure rule, so that if you turn aside from it but a very little, you are out of the right course. Hence, as the Corinthians had deviated from this rule, he calls them back to it. It is a passage that ought to be carefully observed, as showing that there is no remedy for correcting and purging out abuses, short of a return to God’s pure institution. Thus the Lord himself — when he was discoursing respecting marriage, (Matthew 19:3,) and the Scribes brought forward custom, and also the permission given by Moses — simply brings forward his Father’s institution, as being an inviolable law. When we do this at the present day, the Papists cry out, that we are leaving nothing untouched.
“Que nous gastons tout, et ne laissons rien en son entier;” — “That we are destroying everything, and are leaving nothing entire.”
We openly demonstrate, that it is not in one point merely that they have degenerated from our Lord’s first institution, but that they have corrupted it in a thousand ways. Nothing is more manifest than that their Mass is diametrically opposed to the sacred Supper of our Lord. I go farther — we show in the plainest manner, that it is full of wicked abominations: hence there is need of reformation. We demand — what it appears Paul had recourse to — that our Lord’s institution be the common rule, to which we agree on both sides to make our appeal. This they oppose with all their might. Mark then the nature of the controversy at this day in reference to the Lord’s Supper.
23 I received from the Lord. In these words he intimates, that there is no authority that is of any avail in the Church, but that of the Lord alone. “I have not delivered to you an invention of my own: I had not, when I came to you, contrived a new kind of Supper, according to my own humor, but have Christ as my authority, from whom I received what I have delivered unto you, in the way of handing it over.”
Our Author seems to allude here to what he had said previously, when commenting on 1 Corinthians 4:1, as to the duty devolving on stewards of the mysteries of God. — Ed.
Return, then, to the original source. Thus, bidding adieu to human laws, the authority of Christ will be maintained in its stability.
That night in which he was betrayed. This circumstance as to time instructs us as to the design of the sacrament — that the benefit of Christ’s death may be ratified in us. For the Lord might have some time previously committed to the Apostles this covenant-seal,
“Car le Seigneur pouuoit bien quelque temps deuant ordonner a ses Apostres l’obseruation de ce Sacrement;” — “For the Lord might have on some previous occasion appointed to his Apostles the observance of this Sacrament.”
but he waited until the time of his oblation, that the Apostles might see soon after accomplished in reality in his body, what he had represented to them in the bread and the wine Should any one infer from this, that the Supper ought, therefore, to be celebrated at night and after a bodily repast, I answer, that, in what our Lord did, we must consider what there is that he would have to be done by us. It is certain, that he did not mean to institute a kind of nightly festival, like that in honor of Ceres,
“Vne ceremonie, qui ne peust faire que de nuit, comme les Payens auoyent la feste de Ceres;” — “A ceremony which could only be observed at night, as the heathens held the festival of Ceres.” The time when the festival was held, was in accordance with the peculiar secrecy with which its rites were observed. — Ed.
and farther, that it was not his design to invite his people to come to this spiritual banquet with a well-filled stomach. Such actions of Christ as are not intended for our imitation, should not be reckoned as belonging to his institution.
“Pour partie, ou de la substance de son institution;” — “As a part of his institution, or of the essence of it.”
In this way, there is no difficulty in setting aside that subtilty of Papists, by which they shift off
“Ils se mocquent;” — “They deride.”
what I have already stated as to the duty of maintaining and preserving Christ’s institution in its simplicity. “We will, therefore,” say they, “not receive the Lord’s Supper except at night, and we will therefore take it — not when fasting, but after having dined.” All this, I say, is mere trifling; for it is easy to distinguish what our Lord did, in order that we might imitate it, or rather what he did with the view of commanding us to do the like.
entries.9c2b8981f158ff47201ea223bca3eff63ad44f03: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.11.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.11.24" sID="gen119159" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24.</hi> <hi type="italic">Having given thanks.</hi> Paul observes elsewhere, that every gift that we receive from the hand of God<div eID="gen119160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119161" type="x-p"/>is sanctified to us by the word and prayer. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Tim.4.5">1 Timothy 4:5</reference>.)<div eID="gen119161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119162" type="x-p"/>Accordingly, we nowhere read that the Lord tasted bread along with his disciples, but there is mention made of his <hi type="italic">giving thanks</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.6.23">John 6:23</reference>,) by which example he has assuredly instructed us to do the like. This <hi type="italic">giving of thanks</hi>, however, has a reference to something higher, for Christ <hi type="italic">gives thanks</hi> to the Father for his mercy <note n="674"> <div sID="gen119163" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic"> “</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr">Sa misericorde infinie</foreign>;” — “His infinite mercy.”<div eID="gen119163" type="x-p"/> </note> towards the human race, and the inestimable benefit of redemption; and he invites us, by his example, to raise up our minds as often as we approach the sacred table, to an acknowledgment of the boundless love of God towards us, and to have our minds kindled up to true gratitude. <note n="675"> <div sID="gen119164" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et n’en soyons enuers luy ingrats, mats soyons enflambez a vne vraye recognoissance</foreign>;” — “And may not be ungrateful towards him, but may be kindled up to a true acknowledgment.”<div eID="gen119164" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119165" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Take, eat, this is my body</hi> As Paul designed here to instruct us in a few words as to the right use of the sacrament, it is our duty to consider attentively <note n="676"> <div sID="gen119166" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et bien poiser</foreign>;” — “And ponder well.”<div eID="gen119166" type="x-p"/> </note> what he sets before us, and allow nothing to pass unobserved, inasmuch as he says nothing but what is exceedingly necessary to be known, and worthy of the closest attention. In the first place, we must take notice, that Christ here distributes the bread among the Apostles, that all may partake of it in common, and thus every one may <hi type="italic">receive </hi>his portion, that there may be an equal participation among all. Accordingly, when there is not a table in common prepared for all the pious — where they are not invited to the <hi type="italic">breaking of bread</hi> in common, and where, in fine, believers do not mutually participate, it is to no purpose that the name of the <hi type="italic">Lord</hi>’<hi type="italic">s Supper </hi>is laid claim to.<div eID="gen119165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119167" type="x-p"/>But for what purpose <note n="677"> <div sID="gen119168" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais ie vous prie, a quel propos</foreign>;” — “But for what purpose, I pray you.”<div eID="gen119168" type="x-p"/> </note> are the people called to mass, unless it be that they may <hi type="italic">come </hi>away empty from an unmeaning show? <note n="678"> <div sID="gen119169" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Comme s’il retournoit de voir vne bastelerie inutile et sotte</foreign>;” — “As if they were returning from seeing a useless and foolish mountebank scene.”<div eID="gen119169" type="x-p"/> </note> It has, therefore, nothing in unison with the supper. Hence, too, we infer that Christ’s promise is no more applicable to the mass than to the feast of the Salii; <note n="679"> <div sID="gen119170" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vn banquet de la confrairie des Sacrificateurs de Mars, lesquels les Romains nommoyent Salii</foreign>;” — “To the banquet of the fraternity of the priests of Mars, whom the Romans called Salii.” They received this name from their going through the city <hi type="italic">leaping </hi>and <hi type="italic">dancing</hi>. The feast which they partook of, after finishing their procession, was exceedingly sumptuous. Hence the expression — “<foreign xml:lang="la">Epulari Saliarem in modum</foreign>“ — “to feast sumptuously.” Cic. Att. 5. 9. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen119170" type="x-p"/> </note> for when Christ promises that he will give us <hi type="italic">his body</hi>, he at the same time commands us to <hi type="italic">take and eat of the bread</hi> Hence, unless we obey this command, it is to no purpose that we glory in his promise. To explain this more familiarly in other words — the promise is annexed to the commandment in a conditional way, as it were: hence it has its accomplishment only if the condition also is accomplished. For example, it is written, <hi type="italic">Call upon me</hi>;<hi type="italic"> I will answer thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.91.15">Psalm 91:15</reference>.) It is our part to obey the command of God, that he may accomplish for us what he promises; otherwise we shut ourselves out from the accomplishment of it. <note n="680"> <div sID="gen119171" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Nous reiettons l’effet, et luy fermons la porte</foreign>;” — “We reject its accomplishment, and shut the door against it.”<div eID="gen119171" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119172" type="x-p"/>What do Papists do? They neglect participation, and consecrate the bread for a totally different purpose, and in the meantime they boast that they have the Lord’s body. While, by a wicked divorce, they<div eID="gen119172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119173" type="x-p"/>put asunder those things which Christ has joined together, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.19.6">Matthew 19:6</reference>,)<div eID="gen119173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119174" type="x-p"/>it is manifest that their boasting is vain. Hence, whenever they bring forward the clause — <hi type="italic">This is my body,</hi> we must retort upon them the one that immediately precedes it — <hi type="italic">Take and eat</hi> For the meaning of the words is: “By participating in the breaking of bread, according to the order and observance which I have prescribed, you shall be participants also in my body.” Hence, when an individual eats of it by himself, the promise in that case goes for nothing. Besides, we are taught in these words what the Lord would have us do. <hi type="italic">Take</hi>, says he. Hence those that offer a sacrifice to God have some other than Christ as their authority, for we are not instructed in these words to perform a sacrifice.<div eID="gen119174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119175" type="x-p"/>But what do Papists say as to their mass? At first they were so impudent as to maintain, that it was truly and properly called a sacrifice. Now, however, they admit that it is indeed a commemorative sacrifice, but in such a way, that the benefit of redemption is, through means of their daily oblation, <note n="681"> <div sID="gen119176" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par leur belle oblation qu’ils font tousles iours</foreign>;” — “By their admirable oblation, which they make every day.”<div eID="gen119176" type="x-p"/> </note> applied to the living and the dead. However that may <hi type="italic">be</hi>, they present the appearance of a sacrifice. <note n="682"> <div sID="gen119177" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vne apparence et representation de sacrifice</foreign>;” — “An appearance and representation of a sacrifice.”<div eID="gen119177" type="x-p"/> </note> In the first place, there is rashness in this, as being without any command from Christ; but there is a still more serious error involved in it — that, while Christ appointed the Supper for this purpose, that we might <hi type="italic">take and eat</hi>, they pervert it to a totally different use.<div eID="gen119175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119178" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">This is my body</hi> I shall not recount the unhappy contests that have tried the Church in our times as to the meaning of these words. Nay rather, would to God that we could bury the remembrance of them in perpetual oblivion! I shall state, first of all, <hi type="italic">sincerely </hi>and <hi type="italic">without disguise</hi>, and then farther, I shall state <hi type="italic">freely </hi>(as I am wont to do) what my views are. Christ calls the bread <hi type="italic">his body</hi>; for I set aside, without any disputation, that absurd contrivance, that our Lord did not exhibit the bread to the Apostles, but his body, which they beheld with their eyes, for it immediately follows — <hi type="italic">This cup is the New Testament in my blood</hi> Let us regard it then as beyond all controversy that Christ is here speaking of the bread. Now the question <hi type="italic">is</hi> — “In what sense?” That we may elicit the true meaning, we must hold that the expression is figurative; for, assuredly, to deny this is exceedingly dishonest. <note n="683"> <div sID="gen119179" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ce seroit vne impudence et opinionastrete trop grande</foreign>;” — “This were excessive impudence and obstinacy.”<div eID="gen119179" type="x-p"/> </note> Why then is the term <hi type="italic">body </hi>applied to the bread? All, I think, will allow that it is for the same reason that John calls the Holy Spirit a <hi type="italic">dove</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.1.32">John 1:32</reference>.) Thus far we are agreed. Now the reason why the Spirit was so called was this — that he had appeared in the form of a dove. Hence the name of the Spirit is transferred to the visible sign. Why should we not maintain that there is here a similar instance of metonymy, and that the term <hi type="italic">body </hi>is applied to the bread, as being the sign and symbol of it? If any are of a different opinion they will forgive me; but it appears to me to be an evidence of a contentious spirit, to dispute pertinaciously on this point. I lay it down, then, as a settled point, that there is here a sacramental form of expression, <note n="684"> <div sID="gen119180" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est a dire, qui est ordinaire en matiere des Sacremens</foreign>;” — “That is to say, what is usual in connection with Sacraments.”<div eID="gen119180" type="x-p"/> </note> in which the Lord gives to the sign the name of the thing signified.<div eID="gen119178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119181" type="x-p"/>We must now proceed farther, and inquire as to the reason of the metonymy. Here I reply, that the name of the thing signified is not applied to the sign simply as being a representation of it, but rather as being a symbol of it, <note n="685"> <div sID="gen119182" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vn gage et tesmoignage externe</foreign>;” — “An outward token and evidence.”<div eID="gen119182" type="x-p"/> </note> by which the reality is presented to us. For I do not allow the force of those comparisons which some borrow from profane or earthly things; for there is a material <hi type="italic">difference </hi>between them and the sacraments of our Lord. The statue of Hercules is called <hi type="italic">Hercules</hi>, but what have we there but a bare, empty representation? On the other hand the Spirit is called a <hi type="italic">dove</hi>, as being a sure pledge of the invisible presence of the Spirit. Hence the <hi type="italic">bread </hi>is <hi type="italic">Christ</hi>’<hi type="italic">s body</hi>, because it assuredly testifies, that the body which it represents is held forth to us, or because the Lord, by holding out to us that symbol, gives us at the same time his own body; for Christ is not a deceiver, to mock us with empty representations. <note n="686"> <div sID="gen119183" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour penser qu’il nous repaisse d’ombres et vaines figures</foreign>;” — “To think that he would feed us with shadows and empty representations.”<div eID="gen119183" type="x-p"/> </note> Hence it is regarded by me as beyond all controversy, that the reality is here conjoined with the sign; or, in other words, that we do not less truly become participants in Christ’s body in respect of spiritual efficacy, than we partake of the bread.<div eID="gen119181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119184" type="x-p"/>We must now discuss the manner. Papists hold forth to us their system of transubstantiation: they allege that, when the act of consecration has been gone through, the substance of the bread no longer exists, and that nothing remains but the accidents. <note n="687"> <div sID="gen119185" type="x-p"/> By the <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">accidents</hi></foreign> of the bread are meant its color, taste, smell, and shape. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen119185" type="x-p"/> </note> To this contrivance we oppose — not merely the plain words of Scripture, but the very nature of the sacraments. For what is the meaning of the <hi type="italic">supper</hi>, if there is no correspondence between the visible sign and the spiritual reality? They would have the sign to be a false and delusive appearance of bread. What then will the thing signified be, but a mere imagination? Hence, if there must be a correspondence between the sign and its reality, it is necessary that the bread be real — not imaginary — to represent Christ’s real body. Besides, Christ’s body is here given us not simply, but <hi type="italic">as food</hi>. Now it is not by any means the color of the bread that nourishes us, but the substance. In fine, if we would have reality in the thing itself, there must be no deception in the sign.<div eID="gen119184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119186" type="x-p"/>Rejecting then the dream of Papists, let us see in what manner Christ’s body is given to us. Some explain, that it is given to us, when we are made partakers of all the blessings which Christ has procured for us in his body — when, I say, we by faith embrace Christ as crucified for us, and raised up from the dead, and in this way are effectually made partakers of all his benefits. As for those who are of this opinion, I have no objection to their holding such a view. As for myself, I <hi type="italic">acknowledge</hi>, that it is only when we obtain Christ himself, that we come to partake of Christ’s benefits. He is, however, <hi type="italic">obtained</hi>, I affirm, not only when we believe that he was made an offering for us, but when he dwells in us — when he is one with us — when we are <hi type="italic">members of his flesh</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.5.30">Ephesians 5:30</reference>,) — when, in fine, we are incorporated with him (so to speak) into one life and substance. Besides, I attend to the import of the words, for Christ does not simply present to us the benefit of his death and resurrection, but the very body in which he suffered and rose again. I conclude, that Christ’s body is <hi type="italic">really</hi>, (as the common expression is,) — that is, <hi type="italic">truly </hi>given to us in the Supper, to be wholesome food for our souls.
